question: This massive hydro‑electric structure sits on a river that flows through Burkina Faso, empties into the Gulf of Guinea, and creates a reservoir fed by the Oti, Afram, White and Black tributaries. The dam’s reservoir is named after the river itself and lies on the same watercourse that defines the continent’s northern‑hemisphere location. On the summer solstice (June 21) at local solar noon, what is the length of the dam’s shadow in metres, assuming the sun’s declination is 23.44° and using the dam’s official height?

entity_document.title: Akosombo Dam
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>The construction of the Akosombo Dam resulted in the flooding of part of the Volta River Basin and its upstream fields, and in the creation of Lake Volta which covers 3.6% of Ghana's total land area.[2] Lake Volta was formed between 1962 and 1966 and necessitated the relocation of about 80,000 people, who represented 1% of the population.[15] People of 700 villages were relocated into 52 resettlement villages two years prior to the dam's completion; the resettlement program was under the direction of the VRA.[2][3][7][16] Two percent of the resettlement population were riparian fishers, and most were subsistence farmers.[3] The Eastern Region of Ghana and the populations incorporated within its districts were most subject to the project's effects.[17]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The loss of land experienced by the 80,000 people forcibly relocated meant the loss of their primary economic activities from fishing and agriculture, loss of their homes, loss of their family grave sites, loss of community stability, and the eventual loss of important social values.[7] The resettlement program demonstrated the social complexities involved in establishing "socially cohesive and integrated" communities.[7] Insufficient planning resulted in the relocation of communities into areas that did not suit their former way of life and traditions.[7] The loss of the naturally fertile soils beneath Lake Volta impacted traditional farming practices.[7] The poor living conditions provided within the resettlement villages is evident from the reductions in population since resettlement.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>One resettlement village in particular experienced a greater than 50% population reduction in the 23 years following relocation.[7] Increased economic risks and experiences of poverty are associated with those communities most impacted by the Volta River's development.[2] The extensive human migration and degradation of natural resources within the Volta-basin area are caused by poverty in conjunction with population pressure.[19]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The Akosombo Dam, also known as the Volta Dam, is a hydroelectric dam on the Volta River in southeastern Ghana in the Akosombo gorge and part of the Volta River Authority.[1] The construction of the dam flooded part of the Volta River Basin and led to the subsequent creation of Lake Volta.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Lake Volta is the largest man-made lake in the world by surface area.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It covers 8,502 square kilometres (3,283 sq mi), which is 3.6% of Ghana's land area.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>With a volume of 148 cubic kilometers, Lake Volta is the world's third-largest man-made lake by volume; the largest being Lake Kariba which contains 185 cubic kilometers of water.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Increased human migration within the area has been driven by poverty and unfavorable resettlement conditions.[7][19] This migration exacerbated the spread of HIV and has led to its heightened prevalence within Volta Basin communities.[17] The districts of Manya Krobo and Yilo Krobo, which lie within the southwest portion of the Volta Basin, are predominantly indigenous communities and they have a disproportionate prevalence of HIV,[17] showing how local factors have impacted these districts.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Commercial sex work blossomed in response to the thousands of male workers that were in the area to build the dam.[17] Ten percent of the females of child-bearing age from these two districts migrated out of their districts during this time.[17] In 1986, "90% of AIDS victims in Ghana were women, and 96% of them had recently lived outside the country".[17]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In the beginning of 2007, concerns were expressed over the electricity supply from the dam because of low water levels in the Lake Volta reservoir.[20] During the latter half of 2007, much of this concern abated when heavy rain fell in the catchment area of Volta River.[21] In 2010, the highest-ever water level was recorded at the dam.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This necessitated the opening of the flood gates at a reservoir elevation of 84.45 m (277 ft) and, for several weeks, water was spilled from the lake, causing some flooding downstream.[22]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Reservoir-induced seismicity has been recorded because of the crustal re-adjustments from the added weight of the water within Lake Volta.[7] There is an eastward shift of the river's mouth from the changes to the river's delta, and this has led to continuing coastal erosion.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The changes in the river hydrology have altered the local heat budget which has caused microclimatic changes such as decreasing rain and higher mean monthly temperatures. All of these larger scale environmental impacts compound the problems surrounding disruptions to local economic activities and the associated difficult human welfare conditions.[7] A case study by the International Federation of Surveyors indicated that the dam has had a significant impact on the shoreline erosion of the barrier separating the Keta Lagoon from the sea. Dr. <<A_RELEVANT>>Isaac Boateng has calculated the reduction of fluvial sediment as being from 71 million cubic metres per year to as little as 7 million cubic metres per year.[24]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The White Volta or Nakambé (French: Volta blanche) is the headstream of the Volta River, Ghana's main waterway.[1][2] The White Volta emerges in northern Burkina Faso, flows through Northern Ghana and empties into Lake Volta in Ghana.[1] The White Volta's main tributaries are the Black Volta and the Red Volta.[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Volta River
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The three main parts of the river are the Black Volta, the White Volta, and the Red Volta.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the northwest, the Black Volta forms the international borders of the Ivory Coast, Ghana, and Burkina Faso.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Volta flows southward along the Akwapim-Togoland highlands, and empties into the Atlantic Ocean at the Gulf of Guinea at Ada Foah.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>One of its smaller tributaries, the Oti River, enters Ghana from Togo in the east.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Volta River has been dammed at Akosombo for generating hydroelectricity.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The reservoir named Lake Volta stretches from Akosombo Dam in the south to the northern part of the country, and is the largest man-made reservoir by area in the world.[4]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Lake Volta is a reservoir impounded by the Akosombo Dam on the lower Volta River in southern Ghana.<</QA_RELEVANT>> It is one of the largest reservoirs in the world. <<A_RELEVANT>>It extends from the Akosombo Dam in southeastern Ghana to the town of Yapei in the Central Gonja District, Northern Region of Ghana, some 400 kilometres (250 mi) to the north.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Volta River (Akan: Asuo Firaw, Ewe: Amuga, French: Fleuve Volta) is the main river system in the West African country of Ghana.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It flows south into Ghana from the Bobo-Dioulasso highlands of Burkina Faso.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The depth of the river is about 45 feet (14 m) below Lake Volta.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The Volta River is crossed by the Adome Bridge just below the Akosombo Dam.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Impacts of the Akosombo Hydroelectric Project — environmental and human health issues from the Akosombo Dam and Lake Volta.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The country of Burkina Faso was formerly called Upper Volta, after the river.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The dam's power plant generates electricity for the Volta River Authority, and the reservoir also provides water transport routes.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It is a resource for irrigation and fish farming.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Volta River was named by Portuguese gold traders in Ghana.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It was their furthest extent of exploration before returning (volta is Portuguese for "twist" or "turn").[6] It has been known as the "River of return" (perhaps because it was where ships turned around and headed for home) or "river of the bend", in reference to its curved course.[6][7]

property_documents.title: Lake Volta
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Lake Volta lies along the prime meridian, six degrees north of the Equator.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The lake's northernmost point is close to the town of Yapei, and its southernmost extreme is at the Akosombo Dam, 520 km (320 mi) downstream from Yapei.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Akosombo Dam holds back both the White Volta River and the Black Volta River, which formerly converged where the middle of the reservoir now lies, to form the single Volta River.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The present Volta River flows from the outlets of the dam's powerhouse and spillways to the Atlantic Ocean in southern Ghana.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Lake Volta (French: Lac Volta), the largest artificial reservoir in the world based on surface area, is contained behind the Akosombo Dam which generates a substantial amount of Ghana's electricity.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It is completely within the country of Ghana and has a surface area of 8,502 square kilometres (3,283 sq mi).[1] It extends from Akosombo in the south to the northern part of the country.[2][3]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The Akosombo Dam produces 912 MW of electricity for the country, as well as for export to Togo, Benin, and other nearby countries, thereby earning foreign exchange.[1] Lake Volta is also important for transportation, providing a waterway for both ferries and cargo watercraft.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Since the huge lake lies in a tropical area, the water remains warm year-round naturally.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Given good management, Lake Volta is the location of a vast population of fish and large fisheries.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The lake was formed by the Akosombo Dam, which was originally conceived by the geologist Albert Ernest Kitson during the British colonial period in 1915, to exploit the river's energy for smelting locally-sourced bauxite.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The idea regained prominence at the end of the colonial era after World War II when Kwame Nkrumah became president of the Gold Coast colony and began striving for modernization of the land. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The British and local governments formed a joint preparatory commission, which concluded that over 60,000 people would need to be relocated.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, the commission also noted that the lake would boost opportunities for fishing, thereby helping to feed the population in the region.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>On the other hand, issues with water-related illnesses were predicted, such as malaria, trypanosomiasis, schistosomiasis, and onchocerciasis.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In the long run, the formation of the lake disrupted traditional fishing and farming practices in the region and caused a large spike in disease prevalence.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Government-led modernization did not succeed, and people had to adapt to the new circumstances themselves.[5] However, regional food production intensified in the decades after the construction of Akosombo dam, and the lake also opened a large navigable pathway to the north of the country and provided new opportunities for the development of tourism, which is gaining in prominence.<</QA_RELEVANT>> On the other hand, the water level has been decreasing recently because of global warming, reducing power generation.[6]

Aluminium Limited, the main industrial sponsor of the project, withdrew after Ghana became independent in 1957. Revised plans dropped the idea of an integrated aluminium industry and proposed smelting imported bauxite instead. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Kaiser Aluminum entered the project at this point, and after protracted negotiations, funding for the project was secured, but now without regard to the residents of the impacted area as a cost-cutting measure.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Construction thus began before the government started planning the resettlement. Soon after, a public agency was established, and organized construction of 52 replacement towns, which were envisaged to serve as a model for modernization and improving the livelihood of the local population. But because of the rush, the resettlement in 1964 turned out to be chaotic and inefficient. Poor organization caused significant hardship to the local population and led to the issues continuing long after the project's completion.[5] Together, 15,000 homes in 740 villages were flooded, necessitating the resettlement of 78,000 people.[1]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The lake also attracts tourism, and tourist cruises visit the island of Dodi.[4] Dodi Island has become a major tourist site in Ghana since its formation in 1961 following the construction of Lake Volta.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2011, the Volta River Authority allocated US$2.5 million to develop Dodi Island’s eco-tourism potential through its hospitality subsidiary, Volta Hotels Limited.[7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Recent developments include a large-scale enterprise to harvest submerged timber from the flooded forests under Lake Volta.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This project harvests high-value tropical hardwood without requiring additional logging or destruction of existing forest and, according to Wayne Dunn, "could generate the largest source of environmentally sustainable natural tropical hardwood in the world."[8] In addition to generating foreign currency for the region and reducing the dependence of locals on fishing as a primary economic activity, the removal of submerged trees is improving navigation on the lake and increasing safety.[8]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Oti River
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Oti River is about 520 km (323 mi) long.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its headwaters are in Benin and Burkina Faso, it flows through Benin and Togo and joins the Volta River in Ghana.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Tributaries on the left bank in Togo originate from the Togo Mountains to the south. <<Q_RELEVANT>>One of its eastern tributaries is the Kara River, the confluence being on the Ghana–Togo border, where another tributary, the Koumongou River, joins from the south.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The mouth of the Oti was formerly on the Volta River, but it now flows into Lake Volta reservoir in Ghana.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Oti River or Pendjari River (French: Rivière Pendjari) is an international river in West Africa.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It rises in Benin, forms the border between Benin and Burkina Faso, flows through Togo, and joins the Volta River in Ghana.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The river crosses the northern part of Togo in a savannah-clad valley some 40 or 50 km (25 or 31 mi) wide. Along the margins of the river is gallery forest which floods periodically. The dry season here lasts from about November until April, with the hot dry Harmattan wind blowing from the north. At this time of the year the river's flow is minimal. Both the Oti and the Koumongou have floodplains, some 10 and 4 km (6.2 and 2.5 mi) wide, respectively. <<Q_RELEVANT>>These flood extensively during the wet season, but during the dry season they become dry, dusty plains, with the occasional pond or lake in a depression.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Cattle graze on the floodplains during the dry season. There is also some small-scale growing of crops, and the hunting of game takes place there.[3]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The river forms part of the international borders between Ghana, Burkina Faso, Togo, and Benin.[4]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Oti River flows through Pendjari National Park in Benin[5] and the Oti-Kéran National Park in Togo.[3]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The Arctic is a region around the North Pole (90° latitude). Its climate is characterized by cold winters and cool summers. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Precipitation mostly comes in the form of snow.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Areas inside the Arctic Circle (66°34′ latitude) experience some days in summer when the Sun never sets, and some days during the winter when it never rises.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The duration of these phases varies from one day for locations right on the Arctic Circle to several months near the Pole, which is the middle of the Northern Hemisphere.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Between the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer (23°26′ latitude) lies the Northern temperate zone. The changes in these regions between summer and winter are generally mild, rather than extreme hot or cold. However, a temperate climate can have very unpredictable weather.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Its surface is 60.7% water, compared with 80.9% water in the case of the Southern Hemisphere, and it contains 67.3% of Earth's land.[3] The continents of North America and mainland Eurasia are located entirely in the Northern Hemisphere, together with about two-thirds of Africa and a small part of South America.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

During the 2.5 million years of the Pleistocene, numerous cold phases called glacials (Quaternary ice age), or significant advances of continental ice sheets, in Europe and North America, occurred at intervals of approximately 40,000 to 100,000 years. The long glacial periods were separated by more temperate and shorter interglacials which lasted about 10,000–15,000 years. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The last cold episode of the last glacial period ended about 10,000 years ago.[4] Earth is currently in an interglacial period of the Quaternary, called the Holocene.[5] The glaciations that occurred during the glacial period covered many areas of the Northern Hemisphere.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The shadow of a sundial moves clockwise on latitudes north of the subsolar point and anticlockwise to the south.<</Q_RELEVANT>> During the day at these latitudes, the Sun tends to rise to its maximum at a southerly position. Between the Tropic of Cancer and the Equator, the Sun can be seen to the north, directly overhead, or to the south at noon, depending on the time of year. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the Southern Hemisphere, the midday Sun is predominantly in the north.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>When viewed from the Northern Hemisphere, the Moon appears inverted compared to a view from the Southern Hemisphere.[9][10] The North Pole faces away from the Galactic Center of the Milky Way.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This results in the Milky Way being sparser and dimmer in the Northern Hemisphere compared to the Southern Hemisphere, making the Northern Hemisphere more suitable for deep-space observation, as it is not "blinded" by the Milky Way.[citation needed][11]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Northern Hemisphere is the half of Earth that is north of the equator.<</Q_RELEVANT>> For other planets in the Solar System, north is defined as being in the same celestial hemisphere relative to the invariable plane the Solar System as Earth's North Pole.[1]

Due to Earth's axial tilt of 23.439281°, there is a seasonal variation in the lengths of the day and night. There is also a seasonal variation in temperatures, which lags the variation in day and night. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Conventionally, winter in the Northern Hemisphere is taken as the period from the December solstice (typically December 21 UTC) to the March equinox (typically March 20 UTC), while summer is taken as the period from the June solstice through to the September equinox (typically on 23 September UTC).<</Q_RELEVANT>> The dates vary each year due to the difference between the calendar year and the astronomical year. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Within the Northern Hemisphere, oceanic currents can change the weather patterns that affect many factors within the north coast.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Such events include El Niño–Southern Oscillation.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In the Northern Hemisphere, objects moving across or above the surface of the Earth tend to turn to the right because of the Coriolis effect.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As a result, large-scale horizontal flows of air or water tend to form clockwise-turning gyres.[6] These are best seen in ocean circulation patterns in the North Atlantic and North Pacific oceans.[6] Within the Northern Hemisphere, oceanic currents can change the weather patterns that affect many factors within the north coast.[7] For the same reason, flows of air down toward the northern surface of the Earth tend to spread across the surface in a clockwise pattern.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Thus, clockwise air circulation is characteristic of high pressure weather cells in the Northern Hemisphere.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Conversely, air rising from the northern surface of the Earth (creating a region of low pressure) tends to draw air toward it in a counterclockwise pattern. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Hurricanes and tropical storms (massive low-pressure systems) spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.[8]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>As of 2015, the Northern Hemisphere is home to approximately 6.4 billion people, which is around 87.0% of the Earth's total human population of 7.3 billion people.[12][13][14]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.document:
The name Guinea is usually said to have been a corrupt form of the name Ghana, picked up by the Portuguese in the Maghrib. The present writer finds this unacceptable. The name Guinea has been in use both in the Maghrib and in Europe long before Prince Henry's time. <<Q_RELEVANT>>For example, on a map dated about 1320 by the Genoese cartographer Giovanni di Carignano, who got his information about Africa from a fellow-countryman in Sijilmassa [ancient trading city in North Africa], we find Gunuia, and in the Catalan atlas of 1375 as Ginyia.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>A passage in Leo [Africanus] (vol.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>III, 822) points to Guinea having been a corrupt form of Jenne [2,000-year-old city in central Mali on Niger river], less famous than Ghana but nevertheless for many centuries famed in the Maghrib as a great market and a seat of learning.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The relevant passage reads: "The Kingdom of Ghinea . . . called by the merchants of our nation Gheneoa, by the natural inhabitants thereof Genni and by the Portugals and other people of Europe Ghinea." But it seems more probable that Guinea derives from aguinaou, the Berber for Negro. Marrakech [city in southeastern Morocco] has a gate, built in the twelfth century, called the Bab Aguinaou, the Gate of the Negro (Delafosse, Haut-Sénégal-Niger, II, 277–278). The modern application of the name Guinea to the coast dates only from 1481. In that year the Portuguese built a fort, São Jorge da Mina (modern-day Elmina), on the Gold Coast region, and their king, John II, was permitted by the Pope [Sixtus II or Innocent VIII] to style himself Lord of Guinea, a title that survived until the recent extinction of the monarchy.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>São Tomé and Príncipe (officially the Democratic Republic of São Tomé and Príncipe) is a Portuguese-speaking island nation in the Gulf of Guinea that became independent from Portugal in 1975.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is located off the western equatorial coast of Africa and consists of two islands, São Tomé and Príncipe.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>They are located about 140 kilometres (87 mi) apart and about 250 and 225 kilometres (155 and 140 mi), respectively, off the northwestern coast of Gabon.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Both islands are part of an extinct volcanic mountain range. São Tomé, the sizeable southern island, is situated just north of the Equator.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Kidnapping for ransom is also one of the most prevalent maritime crimes in the region.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Between 2018 and 2019, the number of crew members that were kidnapped in the Gulf of Guinea increased by 50%, leading the region to account for 90% of global kidnappings at sea.[7] About 92% of the hostage-taking and 73% of kidnappings happening in and around Africa are happening in the Gulf of Guinea.[8] There is also a large issue of drug trafficking in the Gulf of Guinea and the region has over the last few years become a haven for drug trafficking mainly from South America into Europe.[8]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Gulf of Guinea (French: Golfe de Guinée; Spanish: Golfo de Guinea; Portuguese: Golfo da Guiné) is the northeasternmost part of the tropical Atlantic Ocean from Cape Lopez in Gabon, north and west to Cape Palmas in Liberia.[1] Null Island, defined as the intersection of the Equator and Prime Meridian (zero degrees latitude and longitude), is in the gulf.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Today, the word "Guinea" is found in the names of three countries in Africa (Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, and Equatorial Guinea), and in one country in Melanesia (Papua New Guinea).<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>IUU depletes fish stocks in the area and causes issues for fishermen and the local population food security.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>One of the main issues of IUU is that a lot of the fish that is caught in the Gulf of Guinea is fish that is unreported when caught.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This causes overfishing and overfishing causes depleting fisheries all around the region. IUU fishing also becomes a severe issue in the region because it allows fishermen to fish in vessels that are not nationally regulated or managed. Furthermore, can these vessels threaten people's human security due to poor working conditions and poorly regulated boats? Many of the IUU fishing boats are old, rusty, and often in poor condition.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>"Guinea" is thought to have originated from a local name for an area in the region, although the specifics are disputed.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Bovill (1995) gives a thorough description:[3]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The name "Guinea" was also previously applied to the south coast of West Africa (north of the Gulf of Guinea), which became known as "Upper Guinea", and to the west coast of Southern Africa (to the east), which became known as "Lower Guinea".[citation needed]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Bobowasi Island is an island off the west coast of Africa in the Gulf of Guinea that is part of the Western Region of Ghana.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Multiple institutional mandates address maritime security in the Gulf of Guinea: the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS).[4] Additionally, maritime security in the Gulf of Guinea is also addressed by the Gulf of Guinea Commission (GGC).[4]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Since 2000, nearly 2 million more people have access to water in the four principal urban centres in the country; the company has kept the quality of infrastructure high (less than 18% of the water is lost through leaks – one of the lowest in sub-Saharan Africa), improved financial reporting, and increased its annual revenue by an average of 12% (well above inflation).[174] Challenges remain, including difficulties among some customers in paying for services, with the need to rely on international aid to expand its infrastructure.[174] The state-owned, commercially run venture has helped the nation reach its Millennium Development Goal (MDG) targets in water-related areas, and has grown as a viable company.[174]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The music of Burkina Faso includes the folk music of 60 different ethnic groups.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Mossi people, centrally located around Ouagadougou, account for 40% of the population while, to the south, Gurunsi, Gurma, Dagaaba and Lobi populations, speaking Gur languages closely related to the Mossi language, extend into the coastal states.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In the north and east the Fulani of the Sahel preponderate, while in the south and west the Mande languages are common; Samo, Bissa, Bobo, Senufo and Marka. Burkinabé traditional music has continued to thrive and musical output remains quite diverse. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Popular music is mostly in French.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Burkina Faso has yet to produce a major pan-African success.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>It is made up of two major types of countryside.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The larger part of the country is covered by a peneplain, which forms a gently undulating landscape with, in some areas, a few isolated hills, the last vestiges of a Precambrian massif.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The southwest of the country, on the other hand, forms a sandstone massif, where the highest peak, Ténakourou, is found at an elevation of 749 meters (2,457 ft).<</Q_RELEVANT>> The massif is bordered by sheer cliffs up to 150 m (492 ft) high. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The average altitude of Burkina Faso is 400 m (1,312 ft) and the difference between the highest and lowest terrain is no greater than 600 m (1,969 ft).[citation needed]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Burkina Faso[a] is a landlocked country in West Africa.[1] It is bordered by Mali to the northwest, Niger to the northeast, Benin to the southeast, Togo and Ghana to the south, and Ivory Coast to the southwest.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It covers an area of 274,223 km2 (105,878 sq mi).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2024, the country had an estimated population of approximately 23,286,000.[13] After independence it was called the Republic of Upper Volta from 1958 to 1984.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It was renamed Burkina Faso by then-president Thomas Sankara.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Its citizens are known as Burkinabes, and its capital and largest city is Ouagadougou.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The country owes its former name of Upper Volta to three rivers which cross it: the Black Volta (or Mouhoun), the White Volta (Nakambé) and the Red Volta (Nazinon).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Black Volta is one of the country's only two rivers which flow year-round, the other being the Komoé, which flows to the southwest.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The basin of the Niger River also drains 27% of the country's surface.[citation needed]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>There is debate about the exact dates when Burkina Faso's many ethnic groups arrived to the area.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The proto-Mossi arrived in the far eastern part of what is today Burkina Faso sometime between the 8th and 11th centuries, and accepted Islam as their religion in the 11th century.[26] The Samo arrived around the 15th century.[27] The Dogon lived in Burkina Faso's north and northwest regions until sometime in the 15th or 16th centuries, and many of the other ethnic groups that make up the country's population arrived in the region during this time.[28]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Franco-British Convention of 14 June 1898 created the country's modern borders.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In the French territory, a war of conquest against local communities and political powers continued for about five years. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1904, the largely pacified territories of the Volta basin were integrated into the Upper Senegal and Niger colony of French West Africa as part of the reorganization of the French West African colonial empire.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The colony had its capital in Bamako.

On 2 March 2018, Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin attacked the French embassy in Ouagadougou as well as the general staff of the Burkinabè army. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Eight soldiers and eight attackers were killed, and a further 61 soldiers and 24 civilians were injured.[86] The insurgency expanded to the east of the country[87][88][89] and, in early October, the Armed Forces of Burkina Faso launched a major military operation in the country's East, supported by French forces.[90][91][92] According to Human Rights Watch, between mid-2018 to February 2019, at least 42 people were murdered by jihadists and a minimum of 116 mostly Fulani civilians were killed by military forces without trial.[93] The attacks increased significantly in 2019.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>According to the ACLED, armed violence in Burkina Faso jumped by 174% in 2019, with nearly 1,300 civilians dead and 860,000 displaced.[94] Jihadist groups also began to specifically target Christians.[95][96][97][98]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

question: The vast ice field that stretches across the Patagonian Andes, lying within Bernardo O'Higgins National Park in Capitán Prat Province, is linked to the prominent town of Puerto Natales and is surrounded by peaks such as Monte San Valentín. A weather station located at the ice field’s central latitude records the exact time of sunrise on the summer solstice (June 21) and the local solar noon. Assuming the station’s clock is perfectly synchronized to UTC and neglecting atmospheric refraction, calculate how many hours of daylight the station experiences on that day.

entity_document.title: Southern Patagonian Ice Field
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>The Southern Patagonian Ice Field (Spanish: Campo de Hielo Patagónico Sur), located at the Southern Patagonic Andes between Chile and Argentina, is the world's second largest contiguous extrapolar ice field.[1] It is the bigger of two remnant parts of the Patagonian Ice Sheet, which covered all of southern Chile during the last glacial period, locally called the Llanquihue glaciation.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

In 1994, the Laguna del Desierto dispute was solved which involved territory of the Ice Field; an international tribunal awarded almost the whole zone to Argentina.[13][14] After a refused appeal in 1995, Chile accepted the award. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Since then, Chile has had a small corridor to access Mount Fitz Roy, and the Marconi Pass was defined as an international border crossing point.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Glaciers in the temperate Southern Patagonian Ice Field are melting and rapidly losing mass with the warming global climate.[42] This region is already known for its rapid turnover rate, boasting to the highest flow rates and highest precipitation rates in the world.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Rain and snowfall across the ice field, on average, ranges from two to eleven meters per year from the southern Pacific Ocean.[43] As a result of this dense moisture content, the region has record rates of thinning and retreat.[44] Such rates have unfortunately exacerbated in recent decades, reaching some of the highest across the globe.[42]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Circo de los Altares is an important hiking place.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Section A of the agreement (between Cerro Murallón and Daudet) and a small part of B (from Fitz Roy to a point defined to the west) was drawn; however, they also agreed that section B (from Fitz Roy to Murallón) would wait until completion of a detailed 1:50,000 scale map of the area with further negotiations.<</Q_RELEVANT>> To date, this one section remains the final non-concluded boundary section and has been an irritant in Argentina-Chile relations.

<<A_RELEVANT>>The Southern Patagonian Ice Field section of the border is the last remaining land border issue between Chile and Argentina.<</A_RELEVANT>> On August 1, 1991, the governments of Chile and Argentina agreed on a borderline, but the agreement was never ratified by the Argentine legislature. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Later, in 1998, both governments agreed to redraw the borderline between Mount Fitz Roy and Daudet.[15][16]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The Southern Patagonian Ice Field extends from parallels 48° 15′ S to 51° 30′ S for approximately 350 kilometres (220 mi), and has an approximate area of 16,480 km2 (6,360 sq mi), of which 14,200 km2 (5,500 sq mi) belong to Chile and 2,600 km2 (1,000 sq mi) belong to Argentina.[a]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>An important part of the ice field is protected under different national parks, such as the Bernardo O'Higgins and Torres del Paine in Chile, and the aforementioned Los Glaciares in Argentina.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>There are two known volcanoes under the ice field: Lautaro and Viedma.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Due to their inaccessibility they are among the least researched volcanoes in Chile and Argentina.

The boundary between Argentina and Chile in the area was established by the 1881 treaty and delimited in 1898 by the experts of both countries working in the demarcation of the border, and which differences led to the 1902 award, in which they agreed they did not have differences on the part of the border between Fitz Roy and Stokes. The award is established "to perpetuity" by both countries under British tutelage. <<A_RELEVANT>>The map published by the British Crown, as part of the documentation of the 1902 award, illustrates a clear demarcation line (from the Fitz Roy to the Stokes) to the east of the Southern Patagonian Ice Fields, leaving most of the territory in question in the Chilean side.[9]<</A_RELEVANT>>

The 1902 award considered that in that area the high peaks are water dividing and therefore there was no dispute. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Both experts, Francisco Pascasio Moreno from Argentina and Diego Barros Arana from Chile, agreed on the border between Mount Fitz Roy and Stokes[10] (nowadays Cervantes).[11] Since 1898, the demarcation of the border in the ice field, between the two mountains, was defined on the next mountains and their natural continuity: Fitz Roy, Torre, Huemul, Campana, Agassiz, Heim, Mayo, and Stokes/Cervantes.[5][7][8] In 1914, the Mariano Moreno range was visited by an expedition; however, Francisco Pascasio Moreno already knew of its existence.[12] Argentina started to question the border, arguing that the border should be in the Mariano Moreno range.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Puerto Natales
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Puerto Natales is a city in Chilean Patagonia.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It is the capital of both the commune of Natales and the province of Última Esperanza, one of the four provinces that make up the Magallanes and Antartica Chilena Region in the southernmost part of Chile. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Puerto Natales is the only city in the province.[4] It is located 247 km (153 mi) northwest of Punta Arenas.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is the final passenger port of call for the Navimag ferry sailing from Puerto Montt into the Señoret Channel as well as the primary transit point for travellers to Torres del Paine National Park, Chile.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The province where Puerto Natales is located was named Última Esperanza (Last Hope) by the sailor Juan Ladrilleros, who was seeking the Strait of Magellan in the year 1557.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It was his "last hope" to find the Strait after exploring the maze of channels between the waters of the Pacific and the mainland. It was not until three centuries later, in 1830, that another major expedition sailed through the fjords and channels of Última Esperanza: the British expedition of the sloop HMS Beagle. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Some of the expedition members such as Robert FitzRoy, William Skyring and James Kirke as well as their senior officers are remembered by several place-names in the area.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Commander Fitzroy was the captain during the Second voyage of HMS Beagle (1831–1836).

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Bike trips around Torres del Paine National Park are a quiet way to admire the nature and the majestic sights.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>On horseback you can visit the characteristic farms that dot the countryside around Puerto Natales.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Kayaks offer a quieter alternative to boat trips and are a perfect platform to admire the landscapes of the fjords from a different point of view.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The city was formally founded under the government of Ramón Barros Luco on May 31, 1911. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Nowadays, one of its most important industries is tourism although the cattle and aquaculture industries are also significant.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>While winds, colds and thin soils limit horticulture in Puerto Natales there is still a small-scale local produce of zucchini, cherry tomatoes, strawberries, cucumbers and carrots.[6]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

There are daily LATAM flights from Santiago, Chile's capital city, to the Presidente Carlos Ibáñez del Campo International Airport in Punta Arenas. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The smaller Sky Airline offers direct flights to the Teniente Julio Gallardo Airport near Puerto Natales three times a week.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Overland, Puerto Natales is 3,100 km (1,900 mi) from Santiago, 2,300 km (1,400 mi) from Puerto Montt and 1,600 km (990 mi) from Coyhaique.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The city of Puerto Natales is the capital of the Natales commune and the Última Esperanza Province.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As a commune, Natales is a third-level administrative division of Chile administered by a municipal council, headed by an alcalde who is directly elected every four years.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The 2016-2020 alcalde is Fernando Paredes Mansilla (UDI), and the councilors are:[1][2]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>It is located at the opening of Última Esperanza Sound and was originally inhabited by the Kawésqar or Alacaluf people and the Aoniken or Tehuelche people.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The first Europeans to visit the area where the city is located were the expeditionaries led by Juan Ladrillero, a Spanish explorer who was looking for the Strait of Magellan's western passage in 1557.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

A museum in nearby Punta Arenas. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Nao Victoria was one of the five ships (and the only one that survived) that sailed in the Spanish Armada de Molucca expedition which discovered the meeting point the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.<</Q_RELEVANT>> A realistic, technically and historically accurate replica of the ship commemorates the expedition and allows visitors to experience the historic voyage.[16]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Puerto Natales has many tourist facilities, and it has become a common base for excursions to the world-renowned Torres del Paine National Park, one of the most popular national parks in Chile.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its main feature, the mountainous "towers" ("torres"), are an impressive and unique rock formation known as "Torres del Paine".<</Q_RELEVANT>> They comprise the Torre Central (Central Tower), 2,800 meters high; Torre Sur (South Tower) 2,850 m; and Torre Norte (North Tower) 2,248 m. Named a Unesco World Biosphere Reserve, the park is home to hundreds of different birds and many species of mammals, as well as the third-largest ice field on the planet.[11]

In 1870, interest in the region of Ultima Esperanza was rekindled. Among the daring travelers who ventured to these desolate lands was Santiago Zamora, also known as 'Baqueano' Zamora. <<Q_RELEVANT>>He discovered the lakes of the Torres del Paine area and many wild horses are locally known as baguales.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Another was the English traveler and writer Lady Florence Dixie, commemorated in the city's present-day Hotel Lady Florence Dixie.[7] Dixie wrote the book Across Patagonia, where she relates the first tourist expedition to Torres del Paine (the three granite spires) which she named as Cleopatra's needles.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The Southern Patagonian Ice Field (Spanish: Campo de Hielo Patagónico Sur), located at the Southern Patagonic Andes between Chile and Argentina, is the world's second largest contiguous extrapolar ice field.[1] It is the bigger of two remnant parts of the Patagonian Ice Sheet, which covered all of southern Chile during the last glacial period, locally called the Llanquihue glaciation.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

In 1994, the Laguna del Desierto dispute was solved which involved territory of the Ice Field; an international tribunal awarded almost the whole zone to Argentina.[13][14] After a refused appeal in 1995, Chile accepted the award. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Since then, Chile has had a small corridor to access Mount Fitz Roy, and the Marconi Pass was defined as an international border crossing point.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Glaciers in the temperate Southern Patagonian Ice Field are melting and rapidly losing mass with the warming global climate.[42] This region is already known for its rapid turnover rate, boasting to the highest flow rates and highest precipitation rates in the world.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Rain and snowfall across the ice field, on average, ranges from two to eleven meters per year from the southern Pacific Ocean.[43] As a result of this dense moisture content, the region has record rates of thinning and retreat.[44] Such rates have unfortunately exacerbated in recent decades, reaching some of the highest across the globe.[42]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Circo de los Altares is an important hiking place.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Section A of the agreement (between Cerro Murallón and Daudet) and a small part of B (from Fitz Roy to a point defined to the west) was drawn; however, they also agreed that section B (from Fitz Roy to Murallón) would wait until completion of a detailed 1:50,000 scale map of the area with further negotiations.<</Q_RELEVANT>> To date, this one section remains the final non-concluded boundary section and has been an irritant in Argentina-Chile relations.

<<A_RELEVANT>>The Southern Patagonian Ice Field section of the border is the last remaining land border issue between Chile and Argentina.<</A_RELEVANT>> On August 1, 1991, the governments of Chile and Argentina agreed on a borderline, but the agreement was never ratified by the Argentine legislature. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Later, in 1998, both governments agreed to redraw the borderline between Mount Fitz Roy and Daudet.[15][16]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The Southern Patagonian Ice Field extends from parallels 48° 15′ S to 51° 30′ S for approximately 350 kilometres (220 mi), and has an approximate area of 16,480 km2 (6,360 sq mi), of which 14,200 km2 (5,500 sq mi) belong to Chile and 2,600 km2 (1,000 sq mi) belong to Argentina.[a]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>An important part of the ice field is protected under different national parks, such as the Bernardo O'Higgins and Torres del Paine in Chile, and the aforementioned Los Glaciares in Argentina.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>There are two known volcanoes under the ice field: Lautaro and Viedma.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Due to their inaccessibility they are among the least researched volcanoes in Chile and Argentina.

The boundary between Argentina and Chile in the area was established by the 1881 treaty and delimited in 1898 by the experts of both countries working in the demarcation of the border, and which differences led to the 1902 award, in which they agreed they did not have differences on the part of the border between Fitz Roy and Stokes. The award is established "to perpetuity" by both countries under British tutelage. <<A_RELEVANT>>The map published by the British Crown, as part of the documentation of the 1902 award, illustrates a clear demarcation line (from the Fitz Roy to the Stokes) to the east of the Southern Patagonian Ice Fields, leaving most of the territory in question in the Chilean side.[9]<</A_RELEVANT>>

The 1902 award considered that in that area the high peaks are water dividing and therefore there was no dispute. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Both experts, Francisco Pascasio Moreno from Argentina and Diego Barros Arana from Chile, agreed on the border between Mount Fitz Roy and Stokes[10] (nowadays Cervantes).[11] Since 1898, the demarcation of the border in the ice field, between the two mountains, was defined on the next mountains and their natural continuity: Fitz Roy, Torre, Huemul, Campana, Agassiz, Heim, Mayo, and Stokes/Cervantes.[5][7][8] In 1914, the Mariano Moreno range was visited by an expedition; however, Francisco Pascasio Moreno already knew of its existence.[12] Argentina started to question the border, arguing that the border should be in the Mariano Moreno range.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

question: This volcano began erupting in the Pleistocene, a period that follows the Pliocene and precedes the Holocene, and it lies in the UTC±00:00 time zone that replaced the old UTC−00:44 offset. Its highest point, Hvannadalshnúkur, was first reached by climbers in the early 20th century. From the summit of this volcano, a projectile is fired due north with a speed of 1000 m s⁻¹ and travels a horizontal distance of 5 km. How many metres does the Coriolis effect deflect the projectile from its straight‑line path?

entity_document.title: Öræfajökull
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>The original Norse settlers named the volcano Knappafellsjǫkull (Old Norse: [ˈknɑpːɑˌfelːsˌjɔkolː]; Modern Icelandic: Hnappafellsjökull [ˈn̥ahpaˌfɛlsˌjœːkʏtl̥]; 'knobs mountain glacier').[4]  The current name, Öræfajökull, was eventually adopted after the 1362 eruption.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Geographically, Öræfajökull as the glacier, is considered part of Vatnajökull, and the area covered by glacier is within the boundary of Vatnajökull National Park.<</A_RELEVANT>> There are a number of outlet glaciers in the ice cap within the area of the central volcano which clockwise from north are: Breiðamerkurjökull, Fjallsjökull, Hrútárjökull, Bræðrajökull, Kviarjökull, Hólárjökull, Stórhöfðajökull, Gljúfursárjökull, Rótarfjallsjökull (which has a western branch called Kotárjökull), Grænafjallsjökull, Falljökull, Virkisjökull, Svinafellsjökull and Skaftafellsjökull.[5] While most of the outlet glaciers have reasonably clear catchments, not all do. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Some of the icecap feeds directly into river catchments without a named glacier and this happens between the Hrútárjökull and Bræðrajökull, and the Virkisá river drains a number of glaciers between Rótarfjallsjökull and Svinafellsjökull (see map on this page).[5][6]: 144<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Öræfajökull is located at the southern extremity of the Vatnajökull glacier and overlooking the Ring Road between Höfn and Vík.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It is the largest active volcano in the country, and on the summit crater's north-western rim is Hvannadalshnúkur, the highest peak in Iceland at 2,110 metres (6,920 ft).<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Öræfajökull (Icelandic pronunciation: [ˈœːrˌaiːvaˌjœːkʏtl̥] ⓘ; 'Öræfi glacier' or 'wasteland glacier') is an ice-covered volcano in south-east Iceland.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The largest active volcano and the highest peak in Iceland at 2,110 metres (6,920 ft), it lies within the Vatnajökull National Park and is covered by part of the glacier.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Öræfajökull has erupted twice in historical times, in 1362 and 1728.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>These were explosive silicic eruptions with bulk tephra volumes of 0.1–10.0 km3 (0.024–2.399 cu mi) and jökulhlaups occurred.[2] The deposits closer to the central volcano are rhyolytic but the more distal lava flows which can extend for 20 km (12 mi) from the caldera are alkali olivine basalt and both have been erupted in the Holocene.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>In 1362, Knappafellsjökull erupted explosively, ejecting 10 cubic kilometres of tephra,[8] similar in scale to the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo.[4] The eruption sequence lasted for several months, being from a  medium-potassium alkali rhyolite and has been assigned a VEI of 6 although dense-rock equivalent volume may be less than previous estimates at 1.2 km3 (0.29 cu mi).[7] The wealthy district of Litlahérað was destroyed by floods, pyroclastic flows and ashfall.[8] Sailors reported pumice “in such masses that ships could hardly make their way through it.” Thick volcanic deposits obliterated farmland, and ash travelled as far as western Europe.<</A_RELEVANT>> Forty farms were destroyed.[9] More than 40 years passed before people again settled the area, which became known as Öræfi. <<A_RELEVANT>>The name literally means 'an area without harbour,' but it took on a meaning of 'wasteland' in Icelandic, as the 1362 eruption had drastically altered the environment around the mountain.[10]  The volcano likewise took on the new name Öræfajökull.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The summit caldera of this stratovolcano is 3 km × 4 km (1.9 mi × 2.5 mi) and the volcano is 20 km (12 mi) in diameter.[2] It is the most southern of the volcanoes in the Öræfi volcanic belt (Öræfajökull volcanic belt), which is possibly an embryonic rift parallel and to the east of the Eastern volcanic zone.[7]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Photos of Öræfajökull Archived 2020-10-02 at the Wayback Machine www.Icelandportfolio.com<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>"Öræfajökull".<</A_RELEVANT>> Global Volcanism Program. Smithsonian Institution. Retrieved 3 March 2024.

property_documents.title: First ascent
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>First ascent of Cerro Torre: In 1959, Cesare Maestri claimed he and Toni Egger summited, but that Egger who had the camera, was swept to his death by an avalanche on the descent.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Lionel Terry called it "the greatest climbing feat of all time".[23] Inconsistencies in Maestri's account, and the lack of equipment on the route, led most to doubt his claim.[23]  Maestri further inflamed the controversy by returning in 1970 and drilling 400 bolts onto his new Compressor Route, to claim the second ascent.[23] In 2012, yet more controversy followed when American climbers Hayden Kennedy and Jason Kruk, removed Maestri's bolts, enabling David Lama and Peter Ortner to make the FFA, for which all four won a 2013 Piolet d'Or.[23]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

As all the key tops were summited, the manner or "style" in which each top was reached became important to climbers, and particularly the ability to complete the ascent without the use of any artificial aids, which is called free climbing. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In free-climbing, the term first free ascent (abbreviated FFA) denotes where a mountain or climbing route is ascended without any artificial aid — note that equipment for protection in the event of a fall can be used as long as they did not aid in the climber's upward progression.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Completing the FFA of a climbing route is often called freeing (or more latterly sending) a route, and is highly coveted.

As the sport of climbing developed, additional types of ascent became notable and chronicled in guidebooks and climbing journals. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In mountaineering, and in the sub-discipline of alpine climbing in particular, the first winter ascent is also recorded, given the significantly greater difficulty of the undertaking.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The first solo ascent is also typically noted, although the first free solo ascent is a more controversial aspect, given the concerns about advocating such a dangerous form of climbing. <<Q_RELEVANT>>With the significant rise in female participation in all forms of climbing, the first female free ascent (or FFFA) has also become notable.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

In 2003, Spanish climber Bernabé Fernández proposed Chilam Balam [fr] as the world's first-ever 9b+ (5.15c) route, when the highest grade at the time, Realization, was at 9a+ (5.15a). <<Q_RELEVANT>>As with Fred Rouhling on Akira, his claim provoked a significant backlash from parts of the climbing community and even accusations that he never completed an FFA (the person who belayed him could not be identified to help verification).[27] The route was repeated in 2011 by Adam Ondra who downgraded it,[27] and further repeats reduced its grade to circa 9a+ (5.15a).[28][29]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In mountaineering and climbing, a first ascent (abbreviated to FA in guide books), is the first successful documented climb to the top of a mountain peak or the top of a particular climbing route.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Early 20th-century mountaineers and climbers were mainly focused on reaching the tops of notable mountain peaks (e.g. the eight-thousanders such as Mount Everest) and the tops of iconic climbing routes (e.g. the great north faces of the Alps such as the Eiger) by whatever means possible, and often using considerable amounts of aid climbing and/or with large expedition style support teams allowing them to "lay siege" to the climb.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>First ascent.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The most notable first ascents started with the golden age of alpinism when the main alpine peaks were summited (and often using aid climbing).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the 1930s, the focus moved to the first ascents of the great north faces of the Alps, and the Eiger in particular.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The 1950s saw the first ascents of most of the fourteen eight-thousanders, and Everest in particular.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>By the 1980s, the rock spires of Trango Towers in the Karakoram, and Torres del Paine in Patagonia also had first ascents.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

First winter ascent. The winter climbing season is between December 21 and March 20.[2]  The first winter ascents of the great north faces of the Alps were a coveted prize, particularly the "Trilogy" of the three hardest, the Eiger, the Matterhorn, and the Grandes Jorasses. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The most notable first winter ascents were the Himalayan and Karakoram eight-thousanders,[2] where the hardest, K2, was only summited in winter in 2021 (66 years after its first ascent) and considered a "holy grail" of mountaineering prizes.[3]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>First ascent of Everest: Arguably the most famous case of an unverified first ascent is whether George Mallory and/or Andrew Irvine reached the summit of Everest on the 1924 Everest expedition.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Subsequent Everest expeditions have not been able to answer the question including the 1999 Mallory and Irvine Research Expedition, and the 2007 Altitude Everest expedition.

Stephen Venables (May 2014). <<Q_RELEVANT>>First Ascent.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Cassell Illustrated. ISBN 978-1844037582.

question: This prominent summit lies in the Alpstein, part of the Appenzell Alps, and its slopes are formed primarily of sedimentary rock; the range itself borders the Glarus Alps and the area is administered by the canton of St. Gallen. A 75 kg skydiver with a drag coefficient of 0.8 and a cross‑sectional area of 0.9 m² jumps from the very top of this peak. Using the standard atmosphere to determine the air density at the summit and then applying the usual balance of gravitational and drag forces, what is the skydiver’s terminal velocity in metres per second?

entity_document.title: Säntis
entity_document.text:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Today, the summit is easily accessible by aerial tramway from Schwägalp.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It had been a popular destination for tourists since the mid 19th century. <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, even though many ideas to make the summit more easily accessible existed since those days, it took almost another century for them to materialize.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Many approaches, using various types of railways starting from several nearby towns, were tried, but ultimately failed.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>One project planned to access Säntis from Wasserauen or Unterwasser by rack-and-pinion railway.<</QA_RELEVANT>> While the lower section of this project between Appenzell and Wasserauen was built and is still part of today's active railway network, the rest of it was halted due to a lack of funding. Finally, local businessman Dr. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Carl Meyer of Herisau came forward with the idea to construct an aerial tramway from the base of the mountain, at Schwägalp, and build a mountain road from the nearby town of Urnäsch for easier access to its lower terminal.<</Q_RELEVANT>> On 22 September 1933, his project was ultimately selected for construction and Meyer was awarded with the necessary licences by the federal government. Finally, on 1 July 1935, the aerial tramway started operations. The original cabins were replaced by larger ones in 1960. The entire aerial tramway installation was replaced between 1968 and 1976. In 2000, new cabins were commissioned. <<A_RELEVANT>>The aerial tramway Luftseilbahn Schwägalp-Säntis is one of the most frequented tramways in Switzerland.<</A_RELEVANT>> It has a total length of 2,307 metres (7,569 ft). The altitude gain between the terminals is 1,123 metres (3,684 ft). The journey takes roughly 8 minutes. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The first tramway was constructed from 1933 to 1935.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>At 2,501.9 metres (8,208 ft) above sea level, Säntis (German pronunciation: [ˈzɛntɪs]) is the highest mountain in the Alpstein massif of northeastern Switzerland.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is also the culminating point of the whole Appenzell Alps, between Lake Walen and Lake Constance.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Shared by three cantons, the mountain is a highly visible landmark thanks to its exposed northerly position within the Alpstein massif.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>As a consequence, houses called Säntisblick (English: Säntis view) can be found in regions as far away as the Black Forest in Germany.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Säntis is among the most prominent summits in the Alps and the most prominent summit in Europe with an observation deck on the top.[2] The panorama from the summit is spectacular.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Six countries can be seen if the weather allows: Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Liechtenstein, France, and Italy.[3]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Säntis is located in the Alpstein region, nearly 10 kilometres (6.2 mi) (as the crow flies) southwest of the town of Appenzell and south of Kronberg.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Three cantons meet on Säntis: Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, and St.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Gallen, the mountain being split between the municipalities of Hundwil, Schwende and Wildhaus-Alt St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Johann. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Even though its summit is at only 2,502 metres (8,209 ft) above sea level, the mountain ranks number 13th in the Alps and 29th in Europe in topographic prominence at 2,021 metres (6,631 ft).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Peaks with high prominence often have impressive summit views, even if their elevations are relatively modest, Säntis being a prime example.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Säntis is also the highest mountain of both cantons of Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Located at the peak of Säntis is a 123.55 meter high transmission tower, which was commissioned in November 1997.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The original tower, built in 1955, had to be renovated several times due to the rough weather conditions before finally being replaced. The antenna of the new transmission tower got a fibre-glass enforced plastic layer on the outside in order to prevent ice falling onto the visitors' terrace. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Swiss radio channels such as DRS 1, DRS 2, DRS 3, RSR la Première and RSI Rete Uno are broadcast from the tower.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Swiss television channels such as SF 1, SF 2, SF Info, TSR 1 and TSI 1 are also broadcast from this location.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Mountains of SwitzerlandMountains of the AlpsMountains of the canton of St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>GallenMountains of Appenzell InnerrhodenMountains of Appenzell AusserrhodenTourist attractions in the canton of St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>GallenCable cars in SwitzerlandHighest points of Swiss cantonsAppenzell AlpsTwo-thousanders of SwitzerlandAppenzell Ausserrhoden–Appenzell Innerrhoden borderAppenzell Ausserrhoden–St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Gallen borderAppenzell Innerrhoden–St. Gallen borderUltra-prominent peaks of Europe

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The exposed position of Säntis results in weather conditions normally observed in the high Alps, which means being a typically polar climate (Köppen: ET) with heavy precipitation not found in most of the Arctic.[4] For example, in April 1999, just beneath the summit on the northern snowfield of the mountain, a snow height of 816 cm (321 in) was recorded.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The daily mean temperature is −0.7 °C (30.7 °F) with a precipitation of 2,840 mm (112 in) per year.

property_documents.title: Canton of St. Gallen
property_documents.document:
The main rivers of the canton are the Rhine (Alpine Rhine), Thur (forming the Thur waterfalls), Linth and Seez. Other rivers in the canton are the Jona, Seerenbach (forming the Seerenbach Falls), Necker, Sitter, Saar and Tamina. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The topography changes from the plains near river Rhine, the Swiss Plateau and Lake Constance, towards the mountainous areas of the Alps in the south (Appenzell Alps and Glarus Alps), which includes also part of the Alpstein massif.<</Q_RELEVANT>> About one third (619.7 square kilometers / 239.3 sq mi) of the canton is wooded, while nearly half of it (9,790.6 km2 / 3,780.2 sq mi) is used for farming. 278.6 km2 (107.6 sq mi) of the farm land is Alpine pastures. Of the rest of the canton, 259.1 km2 (100.0 sq mi) is considered unproductive, while 176 km2 (68 sq mi) is filled with housing or roads.[9]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The mountains of the canton include part of a thrust fault that was declared a geologic UNESCO World Heritage Site, under the name Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona, in 2008.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Churfirsten is located entirely within the canton of St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Gallen and features a cave, the Wildenmannlisloch.

The canton of St. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Gallen is located in the north east of Switzerland and is part of the Eastern Switzerland region.<</Q_RELEVANT>> To the north-east, the canton borders Lake Constance (Bodensee). To the east lies the Alpine Rhine Valley, with the Alpine Rhine and "Old Rhine" representing the borders with Austria (state of Vorarlberg) and Liechtenstein. To the south, the canton is bounded by the cantons of the Grisons (Graubünden), Glarus and Schwyz. To the west lies the canton of Zurich and to the north and west the canton of Thurgau. The two cantons of Appenzell Innerrhoden and Appenzell Ausserrhoden are completely surrounded by the territory of the canton of St. Gallen.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Located in northeastern Switzerland, the canton has an area of 2,026 km2 (782 sq mi) (5% of Switzerland) and a resident population close to half a million as of 2015 (6% of Switzerland).<</Q_RELEVANT>> It was formed in 1803 as a conflation of the city of St. Gallen, the territories of the Abbey of St. Gall and various former subject territories of the Old Swiss Confederacy.

The Tabula Peutingeriana shows a Roman road and a settlement, Ad Rhenum (around present-day Rheineck/St. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Margrethen),[6] near the southern coast of Lake Constance.[7] Centum Prata was a Roman vicus, now located in the municipality of Rapperswil-Jona.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The Strahlegg ruin [de], a Roman watchtower in the municipality of Amden, dates back to 15 BC.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The land elevation above the sea-level varies from 398 m / 1,306 ft (Lake Constance) to 3,251 m / 10,666 ft (the Ringelspitz).<</Q_RELEVANT>> The canton includes portions of Lake Constance (54 km2 / 21 sq mi), the Walensee (rather over 18 km2 / 6.9 sq mi), and Lake Zurich (10 km2 / 3.9 sq mi; mostly Obersee), and several small lakes and reservoirs wholly within its limits (e.g. Gigerwaldsee, Gübsensee, Murgseen, Schwarzsee, Schwendisee, Voralpsee).[10] The only (named) island in the canton is the Schnittlauchinsel in the Walensee.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Agricultural activity consists predominantly of dairy farming and cattle breeding in the mountainous areas.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In the plains fruit and wine production are important, but there is also mixed farming. Industries of the canton include optical goods, pyrotechnics, chemicals and pharmaceuticals.

Tourism plays an important role in the many resorts and a great number of winter sports facilities (Amden, Degersheim, Nesslau, Flumserberg, Pizol, Wildhaus-Alt St. Johann). Atzmännig [de],[17] near Eschenbach, and Flumserberg are summer and winter sports areas, both featuring summer toboggans and a ski areas. There is a thermal spa in Bad Ragaz and another one in St. Margrethen. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Quinten, located on the steep slope on the northern shore of Walensee (Lake Walen), is a car-free village and a popular hiking area.[18][19]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Several cable cars and two funiculars (Iltiosbahn, Mühleggbahn) provide access to mountains.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The canton is served by St. Gallen–Altenrhein Airport, which provides direct routes to Vienna in Austria and to some European destinations which are operated by People's airlines. <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, Zurich Airport is frequently used by air travellers from the canton which provides most domestic and international destinations.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The canton is traversed by the following motorways: A1 in the north, A3 in the south, A13 (Hauptstrasse 13) in the east, A15 in the west. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Mountain passes are Foo Pass, Hulftegg Pass, Oberricken Pass, Ricken Pass, Riseten Pass, Ruppen Pass, Schwägalp Pass, St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Anton Pass, and Wildhaus Pass.

In the Helvetic Republic (1798–1803), the northern parts of the modern canton of St. <<A_RELEVANT>>Gallen, together with Appenzell, became the canton of Säntis (named after the Säntis), while its southern parts, together with Glarus and parts of Schwyz, became the canton of Linth (named after the river Linth).<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Today, the summit is easily accessible by aerial tramway from Schwägalp.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It had been a popular destination for tourists since the mid 19th century. <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, even though many ideas to make the summit more easily accessible existed since those days, it took almost another century for them to materialize.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Many approaches, using various types of railways starting from several nearby towns, were tried, but ultimately failed.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>One project planned to access Säntis from Wasserauen or Unterwasser by rack-and-pinion railway.<</QA_RELEVANT>> While the lower section of this project between Appenzell and Wasserauen was built and is still part of today's active railway network, the rest of it was halted due to a lack of funding. Finally, local businessman Dr. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Carl Meyer of Herisau came forward with the idea to construct an aerial tramway from the base of the mountain, at Schwägalp, and build a mountain road from the nearby town of Urnäsch for easier access to its lower terminal.<</Q_RELEVANT>> On 22 September 1933, his project was ultimately selected for construction and Meyer was awarded with the necessary licences by the federal government. Finally, on 1 July 1935, the aerial tramway started operations. The original cabins were replaced by larger ones in 1960. The entire aerial tramway installation was replaced between 1968 and 1976. In 2000, new cabins were commissioned. <<A_RELEVANT>>The aerial tramway Luftseilbahn Schwägalp-Säntis is one of the most frequented tramways in Switzerland.<</A_RELEVANT>> It has a total length of 2,307 metres (7,569 ft). The altitude gain between the terminals is 1,123 metres (3,684 ft). The journey takes roughly 8 minutes. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The first tramway was constructed from 1933 to 1935.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>At 2,501.9 metres (8,208 ft) above sea level, Säntis (German pronunciation: [ˈzɛntɪs]) is the highest mountain in the Alpstein massif of northeastern Switzerland.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is also the culminating point of the whole Appenzell Alps, between Lake Walen and Lake Constance.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Shared by three cantons, the mountain is a highly visible landmark thanks to its exposed northerly position within the Alpstein massif.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>As a consequence, houses called Säntisblick (English: Säntis view) can be found in regions as far away as the Black Forest in Germany.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Säntis is among the most prominent summits in the Alps and the most prominent summit in Europe with an observation deck on the top.[2] The panorama from the summit is spectacular.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Six countries can be seen if the weather allows: Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Liechtenstein, France, and Italy.[3]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Säntis is located in the Alpstein region, nearly 10 kilometres (6.2 mi) (as the crow flies) southwest of the town of Appenzell and south of Kronberg.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Three cantons meet on Säntis: Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, and St.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Gallen, the mountain being split between the municipalities of Hundwil, Schwende and Wildhaus-Alt St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Johann. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Even though its summit is at only 2,502 metres (8,209 ft) above sea level, the mountain ranks number 13th in the Alps and 29th in Europe in topographic prominence at 2,021 metres (6,631 ft).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Peaks with high prominence often have impressive summit views, even if their elevations are relatively modest, Säntis being a prime example.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Säntis is also the highest mountain of both cantons of Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Located at the peak of Säntis is a 123.55 meter high transmission tower, which was commissioned in November 1997.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The original tower, built in 1955, had to be renovated several times due to the rough weather conditions before finally being replaced. The antenna of the new transmission tower got a fibre-glass enforced plastic layer on the outside in order to prevent ice falling onto the visitors' terrace. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Swiss radio channels such as DRS 1, DRS 2, DRS 3, RSR la Première and RSI Rete Uno are broadcast from the tower.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Swiss television channels such as SF 1, SF 2, SF Info, TSR 1 and TSI 1 are also broadcast from this location.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The exposed position of Säntis results in weather conditions normally observed in the high Alps, which means being a typically polar climate (Köppen: ET) with heavy precipitation not found in most of the Arctic.[4] For example, in April 1999, just beneath the summit on the northern snowfield of the mountain, a snow height of 816 cm (321 in) was recorded.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The daily mean temperature is −0.7 °C (30.7 °F) with a precipitation of 2,840 mm (112 in) per year.

property_documents.title: Glarus Alps
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Glarus Alps (German: Glarner Alpen) are a mountain range in central Switzerland.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>They are bordered by the Uri Alps and the Schwyz Alps to the west, the Lepontine Alps to the south, the Appenzell Alps to the northeast.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The eastern part of the Glarus Alps contains a major thrust fault that was declared a geologic UNESCO World Heritage Site (the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona).<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Mountain ranges of SwitzerlandLandforms of the canton of GlarusCanton of Glarus–Grisons borderGrisons–Canton of Uri borderGrisons–Canton of St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Gallen borderGlarus–St. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Gallen borderMountain ranges of the AlpsSwiss AlpsWestern Alps<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Tödi, the highest of the range and of north-eastern Switzerland (3,614 m), is attended by numerous secondary peaks that arise from the extensive snow-fields surrounding the central mountain.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>A very considerable outlyer, whose chief summits are the Schärhorn and the Gross Windgällen, belonging to the canton of Uri, is connected with the Tödi by the range of the Clariden Grat, north to the Hüfi Glacier.<</Q_RELEVANT>> A less important branch encloses the Biferten Glacier, and terminates in the Selbsanft, south of Tierfehd. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Towards the valley of the Vorderrhein a high promontory stretches nearly due south from the central peaks of the Tödi, and is crowned by the summit of the Piz Posta Biala.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Another considerable ramification of the same mass terminates farther to the east in the peak of the Cavistrau.[1]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The main chain of the Glarus Alps can be divided into six minor groups, separated from each other by passes, the lowest of which exceeds 7,500 ft.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The westernmost of these is the Crispalt, a rugged range including many peaks of nearly equal height.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The highest of these are the Piz Giuv (3,096 m) and Piz Nair. The name Crispalt is given to a southern, but secondary, peak of Piz Giuv, measuring 3,070 m. West of the main group is the Rienzenstock, while a northern outlier culminates in the Bristen. <<Q_RELEVANT>>East of the Crispalt, the Chrüzli Pass separates this from the rather higher mass of the Oberalpstock (3,328 m).[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The eastern limit of the latter group is marked by the Segnas Pass [de] — the most frequented of those connecting the Canton Glarus with the Vorderrhein — beyond which arises a wide-stretching mass of rock and glacier, which is part of the Glarus thrust and culminates at Piz Sardona. This mass is cleft by a deep valley — the Calfeisental: one branch, culminating in the Pizol (2,844 m), extends east over Pfäfers, while another, including the highest peak of the canton of St. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Gallen, the Ringelspitz (3,247 m), runs due east to the low Kunkels Pass (1,357 m), separating this range from the Calanda.[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Here occurs a partial break in the continuity of the chain. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The crest of the snowy range connecting the Oberalpstock with the Tödi nowhere sinks to 9,000 feet, but makes a sweep convex to the north, forming a semicircular recess, whose numerous torrents are all poured into the Rhine through the Val Russein below Disentis.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Two glacier passes lead over this part of the chain — one to west, over the Brunnigletscher to the Maderanertal; the other to the north-east, over the Sand Glacier, to the Linthal.[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Kisten Pass separates the Tödi group from the Hausstock, whose summit attains 3,158 m; a branch of this latter group forms the range of the Kärpf in the canton of Glarus.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Hausstock is cut off from the rather lower but more extended mass of the Vorab by the Panixer Pass (7,907 ft).<</Q_RELEVANT>> Numerous summits, of which the Vorab proper and Piz Grisch are the most important, approach very near, but do not quite attain to 10,000 feet.[1]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Glarus Alps extend well beyond the canton of Glarus, including parts of the cantons of Uri, Graubünden, and St Gallen.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Conversely, not all the mountains in the canton of Glarus are part of the Glarus Alps, with those to the north of the Urner Boden and to the west of the valley of the river Linth considered to be part of the Schwyz Alps.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>List of mountains of the canton of St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Gallen
