property_documents.title: Challenger Deep
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The depression is named after the British Royal Navy survey ships HMS Challenger, whose expedition of 1872–1876 first located it, and HMS Challenger II, whose expedition of 1950–1952 established its record-setting depth.[4] The first descent by any vehicle was conducted by the United States Navy using the bathyscaphe Trieste in January 1960.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As of July 2022[update], there were 27 people who have descended to the Challenger Deep.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>On 7 October 2010, further sonar mapping of the Challenger Deep area was conducted by the US Center for Coastal & Ocean Mapping/Joint Hydrographic Center (CCOM/JHC) aboard the 4,762-ton Sumner.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The results were reported in December 2011 at the annual American Geophysical Union fall meeting.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Using a Kongsberg Maritime EM 122 multi-beam echosounder system coupled to positioning equipment that can determine latitude and longitude up to 50 cm (20 in) accuracy, from thousands of individual soundings around the deepest part the CCOM/JHC team preliminary determined that the Challenger Deep has a maximum depth of 10,994 m (36,070 ft) at 11°19′35″N 142°11′14″E﻿ / ﻿11.326344°N 142.187248°E﻿ / 11.326344; 142.187248, with an estimated vertical uncertainty of ±40 m (131 ft) at two standard deviations (i.e. ≈ 95.4%) confidence level.[81] A secondary deep with a depth of 10,951 m (35,928 ft) was located at approximately 23.75 nmi (44.0 km) to the east at 11°22′11″N 142°35′19″E﻿ / ﻿11.369639°N 142.588582°E﻿ / 11.369639; 142.588582 in the eastern basin of the Challenger Deep.[82][83][84][85]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In November 2019, as cruise SR1916, a NIOZ team led by chief scientist Hans van Haren, with Scripps technicians, deployed to the Challenger Deep aboard the 2,641-ton research vessel Sally Ride, to recover a mooring line from the western basin of the Challenger Deep.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The 7 km (4.3 mi) long mooring line in the Challenger Deep consisted of top-floatation positioned around 4 km (2.5 mi) depth, two sections of Dyneema neutrally buoyant 6 mm (0.2 in) line, two Benthos acoustic releases and two sections of self-contained instrumentation to measure and store current, salinity and temperature.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Around the 6 km (3.7 mi) depth position two current meters were mounted below a 200 m (656 ft) long array of 100 high-resolution temperature sensors. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the lower position starting 600 m (1,969 ft) above the sea floor 295 specially designed high-resolution temperature sensors were mounted, the lowest of which was 8 m (26 ft) above the trench floor.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The mooring line was deployed and left by the NIOZ team during the November 2016 RV Sonne expedition with the intention to be recovered in late 2018 by Sonne. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The acoustic commanded release mechanism near the bottom of the Challenger Deep failed at the 2018 attempt.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>RV Sally Ride was made available exclusively for a final attempt to retrieve the mooring line before the release mechanism batteries expired.[112] Sally Ride arrived at the Challenger Deep on 2 November.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This time a 'deep release unit' lowered by one of Sally Ride's winch-cables to around 1,000 m depth pinged release commands and managed to contact the near-bottom releases.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After being submerged for nearly three years, mechanical problems occurred in 15 of the 395 temperature sensors.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The first results indicate the occurrence of internal waves in the Challenger Deep.[113][114]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

question: A celebrated peak that appears in a famous series of woodcut prints, was the site of an eruption named after a historic era, and lies on the Pacific‑facing island of Honshu in Asia is being studied. Assuming a sea‑level pressure of 1013 hPa, a mean atmospheric temperature of 288 K, a molar mass of air of 0.029 kg mol⁻¹, and a universal gas constant of 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, compute the atmospheric pressure in hPa at the summit of this mountain using the appropriate exponential decrease with altitude. Give your answer to two decimal places.

entity_document.title: Mount Fuji
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>Mount Fuji[a] (富士山・富士の山, Fujisan, Fuji no Yama[b]) is an active stratovolcano located on the Japanese island of Honshu, with a summit elevation of 3,776.24 m (12,389 ft 3 in).<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It is the highest mountain in Japan, the second-highest volcano on any Asian island (after Mount Kerinci on the Indonesian island of Sumatra), and the seventh-highest peak of an island on Earth.[1] Mount Fuji last erupted from 1707 to 1708.[7][8]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Mount Fuji is a distinctive feature of the geography of Japan.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It stands 3,776.24 m (12,389 ft) tall and is located near the Pacific coast of central Honshu, just southwest of Tokyo.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It straddles the boundary of Shizuoka and Yamanashi prefectures. Four small cities surround it - Gotemba to the east, Fujiyoshida to the north, Fujinomiya to the southwest, and Fuji to the south - accompanied by towns and villages. It is surrounded by five lakes: Lake Kawaguchi, Lake Yamanaka, Lake Sai, Lake Motosu and Lake Shōji.[42] They, and nearby Lake Ashi in Kanagawa Prefecture, provide views. The mountain is part of Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park. It can be seen more distantly from Yokohama, Tokyo, and sometimes as far as Chiba, Saitama, Tochigi, Ibaraki and Lake Hamana under skies. It was photographed from space during a space shuttle mission.[43]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Pre-Komitake started erupting in the Middle Pleistocene in an area seven km (4+1⁄2 mi) north of Mount Fuji.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After a relatively short pause, eruptions began again, which formed Komitake Volcano.<</Q_RELEVANT>> These eruptions ended 100,000 years ago. <<QA_RELEVANT>>Ashitaka Volcano was active from 400,000 to 100,000 years ago and is located 20 km (12 mi) southeast of Mount Fuji.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Mount Fuji started erupting 100,000 years ago, with Ko-Fuji (old-Fuji) forming 100,000 to 17,000 years ago, but it is now almost completely buried.<</A_RELEVANT>> A large landslide on the southwest flank occurred about 18,000 years ago. Shin-Fuji (new-Fuji) eruptions in the form of lava, lapilli, and volcanic ash have occurred between 17,000 and 8,000 years ago, between 7,000 and 3,500 years ago, and between 4,000 and 2,000 years ago. Flank eruptions, mostly in the form of parasitic cinder cones, ceased in 1707. The largest cone, Omuro-Yama, is one of more than 100 cones aligned NW-SE and NE-SW through the summit. Mt. Fuji also has more than 70 lava tunnels and extensive lava tree molds. Two large landslides are at the head of the Yoshida-Osawa and Osawa-Kuzure valleys.[49]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Mount Fuji is located at a triple junction trench where the Eurasian Plate, North American Plate, and Philippine Sea Plate meet.[47][48] These three plates form the western part of Japan, the eastern part of Japan, and the Izu Peninsula respectively.[49] The Pacific Plate is subducting beneath these plates, resulting in volcanic activity.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Mount Fuji is located near three island arcs: the Southwestern Japan Arc, the Northeastern Japan Arc, and the Izu-Bonin-Mariana Arc.[49] The Fuji triple junction is only 400 kilometres (250 mi) from the Boso triple junction.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

As of December 2002[update], the volcano was classified as active with a low risk of eruption. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The last recorded eruption was the Hōei eruption which started on December 16, 1707 (Hōei 4, 23rd day of the 11th month), and ended about January 1, 1708 (Hōei 4, 9th day of the 12th month).[51] The eruption formed a new crater and a second peak, named Mount Hōei, halfway down its southeastern side.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Fuji spewed cinders and ash that resembled rainfall in Izu, Kai, Sagami, and Musashi.[52] Since then, no signs of an eruption are recorded. <<A_RELEVANT>>On the evening of March 15, 2011, however, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake at shallow depth occurred a few kilometres from Mount Fuji on its southern side.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The current kanji for Mount Fuji, 富 and 士, mean "wealth" or "abundant" and "man of status" respectively.<</A_RELEVANT>> The origins of this spelling and the name Fuji continue to be debated. In Japanese, kanji characters are often applied by sound, and the meaning of the kanji may have nothing to do with the name of the mountain. <<Q_RELEVANT>>It was named Fuji before the kanji was applied to it.[12]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Mount Fuji is widely regarded to have an attractive volcanic cone.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It has been a frequent subject of Japanese art, especially after 1600, when Edo (now Tokyo) became the capital and people saw the mountain while traveling on the Tōkaidō road.<</Q_RELEVANT>> According to historian H. Byron Earhart, "in medieval times it eventually came to be seen by Japanese as the "number one" mountain of the known world of the three countries of India, China, and Japan".[21] The mountain is mentioned in Japanese literature throughout the ages and is the subject of many poems.[22]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>On March 5, 1966, BOAC Flight 911, a Boeing 707, broke up in flight and crashed near the Mount Fuji Gotemba New fifth station, shortly after departure.<</QA_RELEVANT>> All 113 passengers and 11 crew members died, which was attributed to clear-air turbulence caused by lee waves downwind of the mountain. A memorial for the crash victims sits near Gotemba New Fifth Station.[31]

property_documents.title: Hōei
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Hōei (宝永; Kyujitai: 寶永) was a Japanese era name (年号, nengō; "year name") after Genroku and before Shōtoku.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This period spanned the years from March 1704 through April 1711.[1] The reigning emperors were Higashiyama (東山天皇) and Nakamikado (中御門天皇).[2]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Distribution of volcanic cinders and ash falling across central Honshū after the eruption of Mount Fuji in 1707 (Hoei 4).<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>December 16, 1707 (Hōei 4, 23rd day of the 11th month): An eruption of Mount Fuji; the cinders and ash fell like rain in Izu, Kai, Sagami, and Musashi.[4]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Hōei comes from the Old Book of Tang (寶祚惟永、暉光日新).<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>1704 Hōei gannen (宝永元年): In reaction to the Great Genroku earthquake in Genroku 16, the era name was changed to Hōei (meaning "Prosperous Eternity").<</Q_RELEVANT>> The previous era ended and the new one commenced in Genroku 17, on the 13th day of the 3rd month.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>October 28, 1707 (Hōei 4, 4th day of the 10th month): Great Hōei earthquake.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The city of Osaka suffers tremendously because of a very violent earthquake.[3]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>April 28, 1708 (Hōei 5, 8th day of the 3rd month): There was a great fire in Heian-kyō.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>May 20, 1708 (Hōei 5, 1st day of the 4th month): The shogunate introduces new copper coins into circulation; and each coin is marked with the Hōei nengō name (Hōei Tsubo).[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>October 12, 1708 (Hōei 5, 29th day of the 8th month):  Italian missionary Giovanni Sidotti landed in Yakushima, where he was promptly arrested.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>February 19, 1709 (Hōei 6, 10th day of the 1st month): The wife of shōgun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi killed him with a knife, and then she stabbed herself in the heart.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Tsunayoshi's plan to adopt daimyō of Kai as his successor were known by a few inside Edo Castle. The shōgun's wife, who was also a daughter of the emperor, foresaw that this choice of a successor would be very poorly received by many; and she feared that it might result in a disastrous civil war. The shōgun's wife did everything she could to dissuade Tsunayoshi from continuing with such potentially divisive and dangerous plans; and when it became clear that her arguments were in vain, she resolutely sacrificed herself for the good of the country—she killed her husband and then killed herself. She may also have done this as she hated the boy.[5][note 1]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>1709 (Hōei 6, 4th month): Minamoto no Ienobu, Tsunayoshi's nephew, becomes the 6th shōgun of the Edo bakufu.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>August 7, 1709 (Hōei 6, 2nd day of the 7th month): The Emperor abdicates.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>January 16, 1710 (Hōei 6, 17th day of the 12th month): Higashiyama dies.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>July 7, 1710 – March 22, 1711 (Hōei 7, 11th day of the 6th month – Shōtoku 1, 4th day of the 2nd month): Ryukyuan mission to Edo, the largest delegation—168 people—in the Edo Period.[6]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Looking down towards the peak of Mount Fuji and its central crater.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The Hoei Crater, visible to the right of the peak of Mount Fuji, was the location of the 1707 eruption that spewed ash as far as Edo.<</A_RELEVANT>>

Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). Nihon Odai Ichiran; ou, Annales des empereurs du Japon. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Paris: Royal Asiatic Society, Oriental Translation Fund of Great Britain and Ireland.<</Q_RELEVANT>> OCLC 5850691.

question: This towering African summit lies in the Tibesti Mountains, a range composed of sandstone, dacite and basalt, and the continent it belongs to spans time zones from UTC‑01:00 to UTC+04:00 and includes the most populous city Lagos. Assuming an average continental crustal thickness of 30 km, a crustal density of 2750 kg m⁻³ and a mantle density of 3200 kg m⁻³, estimate the depth to the Moho beneath the summit (in km) using an Airy isostasy model. Give your answer to two decimal places.

entity_document.title: Emi Koussi
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>It is a shield volcano with a diameter of 60–70 kilometres (37–43 mi)[16] or 60–80 kilometres (37–50 mi)[12] and an estimated volume of 150 cubic kilometres (36 cu mi)[15]-2,500 cubic kilometres (600 cu mi).[19] The summit of Emi Koussi is formed by two overlapping calderas, which together form a[20] 15-by-11-kilometre (9.3 mi × 6.8 mi) wide[16] elliptical caldera that extends from northwest to southeast.[20] The northern caldera formed first, then the southern caldera which is about 50 metres (160 ft) deeper below the northern one. 400–300-metre (1,310–980 ft) high scarps form the inner margin of the southern caldera,[21] with the floor at an elevation of 2,970 metres (9,740 ft).[22] Before the formation of the calderas, the volcano may have reached a height of 4,000 metres (13,000 ft).<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Emi Koussi has been compared to a Martian volcano, Elysium Mons.[5][23] The caldera rim is cut by one outlet, the Porte de Modiounga,[24] from which gorges emanate into the caldera.[25] The highest point of Emi Koussi lies on the southern rim of the caldera.[9]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Emi Koussi rises to a height of 3,415 metres (11,204 ft) on the southern side of the volcano,[13][14] rising between <1 kilometre (0.62 mi)[15] and 3 kilometres (1.9 mi) above the surrounding terrain[16] and forming the highest summit of the Sahara.[17] It is considered by some astronauts to be the most recognizable landmark on Earth, as seen from orbit.[16] Supposedly the entire Tibesti can be seen from the northern summits.[18]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Emi Koussi has erupted phonolite, trachyandesite and trachyte,[16] as well as mafic rocks like basanite and tephrite.<</A_RELEVANT>> The erupted rocks define two alkaline suites. Phenocryst chemistry and content varies between the various rocks; among the minerals are alkali feldspar, amphibole, biotite, clinopyroxene, olivine, oxides and plagioclase. <<QA_RELEVANT>>Alkali feldspar, apatite, clinopyroxene, olivine, magnetite, mica, nepheline, oxides, plagioclase, quartz, sodalite, titanite and zircon also form the groundmass of microliths in erupted rocks.[34] Magma genesis mainly involved fractional crystallization processes.[31] Rocks from Emi Koussi were used as raw material by Neolithic societies of the region.[35]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Until 5,400 years ago[36] during the African humid period (Holocene), Era Kohor was filled with a 4.1 square kilometres (1.6 sq mi) lake whose water reached a depth of 130 metres (430 ft)[17] and a volume of 0.45 cubic kilometres (0.11 cu mi).[36] It was fed in part by water accumulating in the outer caldera and percolating to Era Kohor.[37] Diatom beds have been found 125 metres (410 ft) above the floor of Era Kohor[38] and in depressions without outlet elsewhere in the caldera,[39] they reach thicknesses of 4–5 metres (13–16 ft).[40] Farther down on the mountain, gullies start appearing at 2,800 metres (9,200 ft) elevation and become deep gorges by 2,000–2,500 metres (6,600–8,200 ft) elevation.[19] Elleboe wadi originates on Emi Koussi,[41] and several streams on the western flank join into the Enneri Miski which drains southwards and disappears south of the mountains.[42] Small pools of water are found around Emi Koussi.[43]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Quaternary volcanism gave rise to the cones on the slopes of Emi Koussi,[20] and the three maars are the most recent vents in the combined caldera,[21] while long lava flows have been interpreted to be the youngest volcanism at Emi Koussi.[51] The most recent volcanic vents show little erosion.[50] Early in the Pleistocene, erosion took place on the flanks of Emi Koussi,[5] and carbonates were deposited in Era Kohor until recent times.[52][53]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Tibesti mountains feature a desert mountain climate.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>There are no weather stations close to Emi Koussi and the stations at lower elevations likely underestimate precipitation at higher elevations,[42] but based on cloud cover data, a yearly precipitation of 80–120 millimetres (3.1–4.7 in) has been estimated for Emi Koussi.[56] Precipitation was higher in the past,it [14] when the African monsoon expanded over the Sahara[17] and drew moisture from the Mediterranean Sea to the Tibesti,[57] The climate reflects both northerly and southerly influences and is distinct from that of the surrounding deserts.[55] There is no evidence of nivation forms on Emi Koussi[58] and the identification of periglacial landforms is questionable,[55] although periglacial activity likely occurred in the Pleistocene and may continue to the present-day.[54] Even during the Pleistocene, no part of the mountain had sub-freezing temperatures through the entire year.[59]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Sandstone
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Most sandstone is composed of quartz or feldspar because they are the most resistant minerals to the weathering processes at the Earth's surface.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Like uncemented sand, sandstone may be imparted any color by impurities within the minerals, but the most common colors are tan, brown, yellow, red, grey, pink, white, and black.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Because sandstone beds can form highly visible cliffs and other topographic features, certain colors of sandstone have become strongly identified with certain regions, such as the red rock deserts of Arches National Park and other areas of the American Southwest.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Sandstones are clastic in origin (as opposed to either organic, like chalk and coal, or chemical, like gypsum and jasper).[6] The silicate sand grains from which they form are the product of physical and chemical weathering of bedrock.[7] Weathering and erosion are most rapid in areas of high relief, such as volcanic arcs, areas of continental rifting, and orogenic belts.[8]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Lithic arenites are characterised by generally high content of unstable lithic fragments. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Examples include volcanic and metamorphic clasts, though stable clasts such as chert are common in lithic arenites.[1] This type of rock contains less than 90% quartz grains and more unstable rock fragments than feldspars.[1] They are commonly immature to submature texturally.[1] They are associated with fluvial conglomerates and other fluvial deposits, or in deeper water marine conglomerates.[1] They are formed under conditions that produce large volumes of unstable material, derived from fine-grained rocks, mostly shales, volcanic rocks, and metamorphic rock.[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Lithic arenites are characterised by generally high content of unstable lithic fragments. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Examples include volcanic and metamorphic clasts, though stable clasts such as chert are common in lithic arenites.[1] This type of rock contains less than 90% quartz grains and more unstable rock fragments than feldspars.[1] They are commonly immature to submature texturally.[1] They are associated with fluvial conglomerates and other fluvial deposits, or in deeper water marine conglomerates.[1] They are formed under conditions that produce large volumes of unstable material, derived from fine-grained rocks, mostly shales, volcanic rocks, and metamorphic rock.[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>When sandstone is subjected to the great heat and pressure associated with regional metamorphism, the individual quartz grains recrystallize, along with the former cementing material, to form the metamorphic rock called quartzite.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Most or all of the original texture and sedimentary structures of the sandstone are erased by the metamorphism.[4] The grains are so tightly interlocked that when the rock is broken, it fractures through the grains to form an  irregular or conchoidal fracture.[26]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Quartz framework grains are the dominant minerals in most clastic sedimentary rocks; this is because they have exceptional physical properties, such as hardness and chemical stability.[1] These physical properties allow the quartz grains to survive multiple recycling events, while also allowing the grains to display some degree of rounding.[1] Quartz grains evolve from plutonic rock, which are felsic in origin and also from older sandstones that have been recycled.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Quartz arenites are sandstones that contain more than 90% of siliceous grains.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Grains can include quartz or chert rock fragments.[1] Quartz arenites are texturally mature to supermature sandstones.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>These pure quartz sands result from extensive weathering that occurred before and during transport.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This weathering removed everything but quartz grains, the most stable mineral.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>They are commonly affiliated with rocks that are deposited in a stable cratonic environment, such as aeolian beaches or shelf environments.[1] Quartz arenites emanate from multiple recycling of quartz grains, generally as sedimentary source rocks and less regularly as first-cycle deposits derived from primary igneous or metamorphic rocks.[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Emi Koussi
property_documents.document:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>It is a shield volcano with a diameter of 60–70 kilometres (37–43 mi)[16] or 60–80 kilometres (37–50 mi)[12] and an estimated volume of 150 cubic kilometres (36 cu mi)[15]-2,500 cubic kilometres (600 cu mi).[19] The summit of Emi Koussi is formed by two overlapping calderas, which together form a[20] 15-by-11-kilometre (9.3 mi × 6.8 mi) wide[16] elliptical caldera that extends from northwest to southeast.[20] The northern caldera formed first, then the southern caldera which is about 50 metres (160 ft) deeper below the northern one. 400–300-metre (1,310–980 ft) high scarps form the inner margin of the southern caldera,[21] with the floor at an elevation of 2,970 metres (9,740 ft).[22] Before the formation of the calderas, the volcano may have reached a height of 4,000 metres (13,000 ft).<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Emi Koussi has been compared to a Martian volcano, Elysium Mons.[5][23] The caldera rim is cut by one outlet, the Porte de Modiounga,[24] from which gorges emanate into the caldera.[25] The highest point of Emi Koussi lies on the southern rim of the caldera.[9]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Emi Koussi rises to a height of 3,415 metres (11,204 ft) on the southern side of the volcano,[13][14] rising between <1 kilometre (0.62 mi)[15] and 3 kilometres (1.9 mi) above the surrounding terrain[16] and forming the highest summit of the Sahara.[17] It is considered by some astronauts to be the most recognizable landmark on Earth, as seen from orbit.[16] Supposedly the entire Tibesti can be seen from the northern summits.[18]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Emi Koussi has erupted phonolite, trachyandesite and trachyte,[16] as well as mafic rocks like basanite and tephrite.<</A_RELEVANT>> The erupted rocks define two alkaline suites. Phenocryst chemistry and content varies between the various rocks; among the minerals are alkali feldspar, amphibole, biotite, clinopyroxene, olivine, oxides and plagioclase. <<QA_RELEVANT>>Alkali feldspar, apatite, clinopyroxene, olivine, magnetite, mica, nepheline, oxides, plagioclase, quartz, sodalite, titanite and zircon also form the groundmass of microliths in erupted rocks.[34] Magma genesis mainly involved fractional crystallization processes.[31] Rocks from Emi Koussi were used as raw material by Neolithic societies of the region.[35]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Until 5,400 years ago[36] during the African humid period (Holocene), Era Kohor was filled with a 4.1 square kilometres (1.6 sq mi) lake whose water reached a depth of 130 metres (430 ft)[17] and a volume of 0.45 cubic kilometres (0.11 cu mi).[36] It was fed in part by water accumulating in the outer caldera and percolating to Era Kohor.[37] Diatom beds have been found 125 metres (410 ft) above the floor of Era Kohor[38] and in depressions without outlet elsewhere in the caldera,[39] they reach thicknesses of 4–5 metres (13–16 ft).[40] Farther down on the mountain, gullies start appearing at 2,800 metres (9,200 ft) elevation and become deep gorges by 2,000–2,500 metres (6,600–8,200 ft) elevation.[19] Elleboe wadi originates on Emi Koussi,[41] and several streams on the western flank join into the Enneri Miski which drains southwards and disappears south of the mountains.[42] Small pools of water are found around Emi Koussi.[43]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Quaternary volcanism gave rise to the cones on the slopes of Emi Koussi,[20] and the three maars are the most recent vents in the combined caldera,[21] while long lava flows have been interpreted to be the youngest volcanism at Emi Koussi.[51] The most recent volcanic vents show little erosion.[50] Early in the Pleistocene, erosion took place on the flanks of Emi Koussi,[5] and carbonates were deposited in Era Kohor until recent times.[52][53]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Tibesti mountains feature a desert mountain climate.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>There are no weather stations close to Emi Koussi and the stations at lower elevations likely underestimate precipitation at higher elevations,[42] but based on cloud cover data, a yearly precipitation of 80–120 millimetres (3.1–4.7 in) has been estimated for Emi Koussi.[56] Precipitation was higher in the past,it [14] when the African monsoon expanded over the Sahara[17] and drew moisture from the Mediterranean Sea to the Tibesti,[57] The climate reflects both northerly and southerly influences and is distinct from that of the surrounding deserts.[55] There is no evidence of nivation forms on Emi Koussi[58] and the identification of periglacial landforms is questionable,[55] although periglacial activity likely occurred in the Pleistocene and may continue to the present-day.[54] Even during the Pleistocene, no part of the mountain had sub-freezing temperatures through the entire year.[59]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Basalt
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Decompression melting can occur in a variety of tectonic settings, including in continental rift zones, at mid-ocean ridges, above geological hotspots,[29][30] and in back-arc basins.[31] Basalt also forms in subduction zones, where mantle rock rises into a mantle wedge above the descending slab.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The slab releases water vapor and other volatiles as it descends, which further lowers the melting point, further increasing the amount of decompression melting.[32] Each tectonic setting produces basalt with its own distinctive characteristics.[33]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Lava flows represent a major volcanic terrain on Io.[111] Analysis of the Voyager images led scientists to believe that these flows were composed mostly of various compounds of molten sulfur.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, subsequent Earth-based infrared studies and measurements from the Galileo spacecraft indicate that these flows are composed of basaltic lava with mafic to ultramafic compositions.[112] This conclusion is based on temperature measurements of Io's "hotspots", or thermal-emission locations, which suggest temperatures of at least 1,300 K and some as high as 1,600 K.[113] Initial estimates suggesting eruption temperatures approaching 2,000 K[114] have since proven to be overestimates because the wrong thermal models were used to model the temperatures.[113][115]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The common corrosion features of underwater volcanic basalt suggest that microbial activity may play a significant role in the chemical exchange between basaltic rocks and seawater.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The significant amounts of reduced iron, Fe(II), and manganese, Mn(II), present in basaltic rocks provide potential energy sources for bacteria.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Some Fe(II)-oxidizing bacteria cultured from iron-sulfide surfaces are also able to grow with basaltic rock as a source of Fe(II).[125] Fe- and Mn- oxidizing bacteria have been cultured from weathered submarine basalts of Kamaʻehuakanaloa Seamount (formerly Loihi).[126] The impact of bacteria on altering the chemical composition of basaltic glass (and thus, the oceanic crust) and seawater suggest that these interactions may lead to an application of hydrothermal vents to the origin of life.[127]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The majority of tholeiitic basalts are formed at approximately 50–100 km depth within the mantle.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Many alkali basalts may be formed at greater depths, perhaps as deep as 150–200 km.[51][52] The origin of high-alumina basalt continues to be controversial, with disagreement over whether it is a primary melt or derived from other basalt types by fractionation.[53]: 65<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Molten basalt lava has a low viscosity due to its relatively low silica content (between 45% and 52%), resulting in rapidly moving lava flows that can spread over great areas before cooling and solidifying.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Flood basalts are thick sequences of many such flows that can cover hundreds of thousands of square kilometres and constitute the most voluminous of all volcanic formations.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Basaltic magmas within Earth are thought to originate from the upper mantle.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The chemistry of basalts thus provides clues to processes deep in Earth's interior.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Basalt is composed mostly of oxides of silicon, iron, magnesium, potassium, aluminum, titanium, and calcium.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Geologists classify igneous rock by its mineral content whenever possible; the relative volume percentages of quartz (crystalline silica (SiO2)), alkali feldspar, plagioclase, and feldspathoid (QAPF) are particularly important. <<Q_RELEVANT>>An aphanitic (fine-grained) igneous rock is classified as basalt when its QAPF fraction is composed of less than 10% feldspathoid and less than 20% quartz, and plagioclase makes up at least 65% of its feldspar content.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This places basalt in the basalt/andesite field of the QAPF diagram.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Basalt is further distinguished from andesite by its silica content of under 52%.[4][5][6][7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The physical properties of basalt result from its relatively low silica content and typically high iron and magnesium content.[15] The average density of basalt is 2.9 g/cm3, compared, for example, to granite’s typical density of 2.7 g/cm3.[16] The viscosity of basaltic magma is relatively low—around 104 to 105 cP—similar to the viscosity of ketchup, but that is still several orders of magnitude higher than the viscosity of water, which is about 1 cP).[17]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Basalt is often porphyritic, containing larger crystals (phenocrysts) that formed before the extrusion event that brought the magma to the surface, embedded in a finer-grained matrix.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>These phenocrysts are usually made of augite, olivine, or a calcium-rich plagioclase,[10] which have the highest melting temperatures of any of the minerals that can typically crystallize from the melt, and which are therefore the first to form solid crystals.[18][19]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Dacite
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The term dacite was used for the first time in the scientific literature in the book Geologie Siebenbürgens (The Geology of Transylvania) by Austrian geologists Franz Ritter von Hauer and Guido Stache.[1][2] Dacite was originally defined as a new rock type to separate calc-alkaline rocks with oligoclase phenocrysts (dacites) from rocks with orthoclase phenocrysts (rhyolites).[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Dacite consists mostly of plagioclase feldspar and quartz with biotite, hornblende, and pyroxene (augite or enstatite).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The quartz appears as rounded, corroded phenocrysts, or as an element of the ground-mass.[3] The plagioclase in dacite ranges from oligoclase to andesine and labradorite.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Sanidine occurs, although in small proportions, in some dacites, and when abundant gives rise to rocks that form transitions to the rhyolites.[4]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In thin section, dacites may have an aphanitic to porphyritic texture.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Porphyritic dacites contain blocky highly zoned plagioclase phenocrysts and/or rounded corroded quartz phenocrysts.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Subhedral hornblende and elongated biotite grains are present. Sanidine phenocrysts and augite (or enstatite) are found in some samples. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The groundmass of these rocks is often aphanitic microcrystalline, with a web of minute feldspars mixed with interstitial grains of quartz or tridymite; but in many dacites it is largely vitreous, while in others it is felsitic or cryptocrystalline.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Dacite usually forms as an intrusive rock such as a dike or sill.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Examples of this type of dacite outcrop are found in northwestern Montana and northeastern Bulgaria.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Nevertheless, because of the moderately high silica content, dacitic magma is quite viscous[9] and therefore prone to explosive eruption. A notorious example of this is Mount St. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Helens in which dacite domes formed from previous eruptions.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Pyroclastic flows may also be of dacitic composition as is the case with the Fish Canyon Tuff of La Garita Caldera.[10]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The process by which dacite forms has been used to explain the generation of continental crust during the Archean eon.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>At that time, the production of dacitic magma was more ubiquitous, due to the availability of young, hot oceanic crust.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Today, the colder oceanic crust that subducts under most plates is not able to melt prior to the dehydration reactions, thus inhibiting the process.[15]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Dacite is relatively common, occurring in many tectonic settings.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is associated with andesite and rhyolite as part of the subalkaline tholeiitic and calc-alkaline magma series.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The word dacite comes from Dacia, a province of the Roman Empire which lay between the Danube River and Carpathian Mountains (now modern Romania and Moldova) where the rock was first described.[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The relative proportions of feldspars and quartz in dacite, and in many other volcanic rocks, are illustrated in the QAPF diagram.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This defines dacite as having a content of 20% to 60% quartz, with plagioclase making up 65% or more of its feldspar content.[5][6][7][8] However, while the IUGS recommends classifying volcanic rocks on the basis of their mineral composition whenever possible, dacites are often so fine-grained that mineral identification is impractical.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The rock must then be classified chemically based on its content of silica and alkali metal oxides (K2O plus Na2O). <<Q_RELEVANT>>The TAS classification puts dacite in the O3 sector.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In hand specimen, many of the hornblende and biotite dacites are grey or pale brown and yellow rocks with white feldspars, and black crystals of biotite and hornblende.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Other dacites, especially pyroxene-bearing dacites, are darker colored.[4]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The formation of dacite provides a great deal of information about the connection between oceanic crust and continental crust.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It provides a model for the generation of felsic, buoyant, perennial rock from a mafic, dense, short-lived one.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Dacitic magma is formed by the subduction of young oceanic crust under a thick felsic continental plate. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Oceanic crust is hydrothermally altered causing addition of quartz and sodium.[11] As the young, hot oceanic plate is subducted under continental crust, the subducted slab partially melts and interacts with the upper mantle through convection and dehydration reactions.[12] The process of subduction creates metamorphism in the subducting slab.<</Q_RELEVANT>> When this slab reaches the mantle and initiates the dehydration reactions, minerals such as talc, serpentine, mica and amphiboles break down generating a more sodic melt.[13] The magma then continues to migrate upwards causing differentiation and becomes even more sodic and silicic as it rises. Once at the cold surface, the sodium rich magma crystallizes plagioclase, quartz and hornblende.[14] Accessory minerals like pyroxenes provide insight to the history of the magma.

property_documents.title: Chad
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Longtime Chad President Idriss Déby's death on 20 April 2021 resulted in both the nation's National Assembly and government being dissolved and national leadership being replaced with a transitional military council consisting of military officers and led by his son Mahamat Kaka.[108][109]  The constitution is currently suspended, pending replacement with one drafted by a civilian National Transitional Council, yet to be appointed.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The military council has stated that elections will be held at the end of an 18-month transitional period.[110][needs update] In October 2022, Déby extended his rule and was sworn in as transitional president after dissolving the Transitional Military Council.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This caused the 2022 Chadian protests, which became one of the most violent in Chadian history.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The protests however, were suppressed with several opposition parties being banned by the government.[111][112] According to 2023 V-Dem Democracy indices Chad is 16th lowest ranked electoral democracy worldwide and 4th lowest ranked electoral democracy in Africa.[113]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Urban life is concentrated in the capital, whose population is mostly engaged in commerce.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The other major towns are Sarh, Moundou, Abéché and Doba, which are considerably smaller but growing rapidly in population and economic activity.[53] Since 2003, 230,000 Sudanese refugees have fled to eastern Chad from war-ridden Darfur.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>With the 172,600 Chadians displaced by the civil war in the east, this has generated increased tensions among the region's communities.[78][79]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Chad's legal system is based on French civil law and Chadian customary law where the latter does not interfere with public order or constitutional guarantees of equality.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Despite the constitution's guarantee of judicial independence, the president names most key judicial officials.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The legal system's highest jurisdictions, the Supreme Court and the Constitutional Council, have become fully operational since 2000. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Supreme Court is made up of a chief justice, named by the president, and 15 councillors, appointed for life by the president and the National Assembly.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The Constitutional Court is headed by nine judges elected to nine-year terms. It has the power to review legislation, treaties and international agreements prior to their adoption.[85][100]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Uneven inclusion in the global political economy as a site for colonial resource extraction (primarily cotton and crude oil), a global economic system that does not promote nor encourage the development of Chadian industrialisation,[135] and the failure to support local agricultural production has meant that the majority of Chadians live in daily uncertainty and hunger.[136][137] Over 80% of Chad's population relies on subsistence farming and livestock raising for its livelihood.[54] The crops grown and the locations of herds are determined by the local climate.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the southernmost 10% of the territory lies the nation's most fertile cropland, with rich yields of sorghum and millet.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the Sahel only the hardier varieties of millet grow, and with much lower yields than in the south.<</Q_RELEVANT>> On the other hand, the Sahel is ideal pastureland for large herds of commercial cattle and for goats, sheep, donkeys and horses. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Sahara's scattered oases support only some dates and legumes.[16] Chad's cities face serious difficulties of municipal infrastructure; only 48% of urban residents have access to potable water and only 2% to basic sanitation.[53][138]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The dominant physical structure is a wide basin bounded to the north and east by the Ennedi Plateau and Tibesti Mountains, which include Emi Koussi, a dormant volcano that reaches 3,414 metres (11,201 ft) above sea level.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Lake Chad, after which the country is named (and which in turn takes its name from the Kanuri word for "lake"[58]), is the remains of an immense lake that occupied 330,000 square kilometres (130,000 sq mi) of the Chad Basin 7,000 years ago.[53] Although in the 21st century it covers only 17,806 square kilometres (6,875 sq mi), and its surface area is subject to heavy seasonal fluctuations,[59] the lake is Africa's second largest wetland.[60]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Chad,[a] officially the Republic of Chad,[b] is a landlocked country in Central Africa.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is bordered by Libya to the north, Sudan to the east, the Central African Republic to the south, Cameroon to the southwest, Nigeria to the southwest (at Lake Chad), and Niger to the west.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Chad has a population of 19 million, of which 1.6 million live in the capital and largest city of N'Djamena.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>With a total area of around 1,300,000 km2 (500,000 sq mi), Chad is the fifth-largest country in Africa and the twentieth largest nation by area.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Lagos
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Lagos (/ˈleɪɡɒs/ LAY-goss;[10][11] Yoruba: Èkó [èkó]), or Lagos City, is a large metropolitan port city in southwestern Nigeria.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As of November 2025[update], the size of the city's population has been estimated to be between 17 and 21 million residents, making Lagos the largest city in Nigeria, the most populous urban area on the African continent,[12][13][14][15][16] and one of the fastest-growing megacities in the world.[17][18] Lagos was the national capital of Nigeria until the government's December 1991 decision to relocate its capital to Abuja, in the centre of the country.[19][20][21] Apart from serving as a major African financial center, Lagos has also played a significant role in the national economy, serving as the economic hub of Lagos State and the entire country of Nigeria.[22][23][24] The city has a significant influence on commerce, entertainment, technology, education, politics, tourism, art, and fashion in Africa.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Lagos is also among the top ten of the world's fastest-growing cities and urban areas.[32][33] A megacity, it has the second-highest GDP in Africa,[2][34] and houses one of the largest and busiest seaports on the continent.[35][36][37] Due to the large urban population and port traffic volumes, Lagos is classified as a Medium-Port Megacity.[38]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Lekki Peninsula shares some prestige with its Ikoyi and Victoria Island neighbours.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Development has stretched the piece of land further such that the Ibeju axis, though closer to Epe (which is on the outskirts of Lagos) is almost always described as part of Lekki.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The expanse of land starts from the Lekki toll gate, which was the focal stage of the famous #EndSars protest in October 2020, and ends in Ibeju-Lekki and boasts of communities slowly inching their way to suburb status such as Ajah, Awoyaya, Sangotedo, Abijo, and Eputu.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>There is quite a bit of place to see – the Lekki Conservation Centre; The Novare Mall; The Lekki Free Trade Zone – Dangote, Africa's richest man is building his refinery in this FTZ; Lagos Business School; Eleko Beach; Elegushi Beach; La Campagne Tropicana – a beach/tourist getaway, Pan-Atlantic University.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The area has a Catholic monastery.[99]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Five Cowries Terminal is the central terminal for ferry operations in Lagos.[288] The terminal is located on the lagoon between Lagos Island and Victoria Island and was commissioned on 30 August 2018.[289][290] Five Cowries also serves as the headquarters of the Lagos State Waterways Authority (LASWA).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It has a jetty, restaurant, bar, administrative offices, ticket offices, waiting area, toilets, lift, conference room, and ATMs.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Boats from private individuals and other operators also dock at the pier.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The terminal also has a multi-storey car park with space for over 800 vehicles.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The multi-storey car park is located behind the terminal (as seen from the lagoon) and is directly connected to the terminal.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The terminal was built without thresholds and there is a toilet for wheelchair users.[288] Five Cowries is open seven days a week, from 8.00 am to 5.00 pm.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The terminal is located next to the Falomo Bridge.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The destinations of LASWA ferries are Marina, Ikoyi, Victoria Island, Lekki, Apapa, Ikorodu and Badagry.[291]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Port of Lagos / Apapa is the oldest and largest port in the country, both in terms of land area and cargo volume handled.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>More than half of Nigeria's maritime trade is handled here, and the port also acts as a transhipment point for landlocked countries such as Chad and Niger.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Around 1,000 ships with 5,700,000 tonnes of cargo call at the Lagos port complex annually.[125]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The population of Metropolitan Lagos is disputed.[48] In the 2006 federal census data, the conurbation had a population of about 9 million people.[49] However, the figure was disputed by the Lagos State Government, which later released its own population data, putting the population of Lagos Metropolitan Area at approximately 16 million.[note 1] Daily, the Lagos area is growing by some 3,000 people or around 1.1 million annually, so the true population figure of the greater Lagos area in 2022 is roughly 28 million (up from some 23.5 million in 2018).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Lagos may therefore have overtaken Kinshasa as Africa's most populous city.[1][40][50][51] The Lagos conurbation is part of an emerging transnational megalopolis on the coast of West Africa that includes areas in five sovereign states, the Abidjan–Lagos Corridor.[52][53]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

question: A spectacular waterfall sits on a river that begins from a massive glacier and eventually empties into a fjord on the north coast of an island nation whose entire drainage basin lies within its borders. The falls are a popular tourist site and are roughly 12 m tall. Assuming the site’s latitude is the same as the waterfall’s location, calculate how long (in metres) the shadow of the waterfall’s crest would be at solar noon on the summer solstice (June 21).

entity_document.title: Goðafoss
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>Goðafoss (Icelandic pronunciation: [ˈkɔːðaˌfɔsː] ⓘ) is a waterfall in northern Iceland.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is located along the country's main ring road at the junction with the Sprengisandur highland road,[1] about 45 minutes from Akureyri.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The water of the river Skjálfandafljót falls from a height of 12 metres over a width of 30 metres.[1] A 1.8-mile hiking trail loops around the waterfall area.[2]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The origin of the waterfall's name is not completely clear.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In modern Icelandic, the name can be read either as "waterfall of the goð (gods)" or "waterfall of the goði (chieftain)." Linguist and placename expert Svavar Sigmundsson suggests that the name derives from two crags at the falls which resemble pagan idols.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1879–1882, a myth was published in Denmark according to which the waterfall was named when the lawspeaker Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði made Christianity the official religion of Iceland in the year 999 or 1000.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Upon returning home from the Alþingi, Þorgeir supposedly threw his statues of the Norse gods into the waterfall. <<QA_RELEVANT>>However, although the story of Þorgeir's role in the adoption of Christianity in Iceland is preserved in Ari Þorgilsson's Íslendingabók, no mention is made of Þorgeir throwing his idols into Goðafoss.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The legend appears to be a nineteenth-century fabrication.[3]  Nevertheless, a window in Akureyrarkirkja, the main church at Akureyri, illustrates this story.

<<QA_RELEVANT>>MS Goðafoss [is] was an Icelandic ship named after the waterfall, it was used to transport both freight and passengers.<</QA_RELEVANT>> It was sunk by the German submarine U-300 in World War II, resulting in great loss of life.[4][5]

property_documents.title: Vatnajökull
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Vatnajökull (Icelandic pronunciation: [ˈvahtnaˌjœːkʏtl̥] ⓘ, literally "Glacier of Lakes"; sometimes translated as Vatna Glacier in English) is the largest and most voluminous ice cap in Iceland, and the second largest in area in Europe after the Severny Island ice cap of Novaya Zemlya.[1] It is in the south-east of the island, covering approximately 8% of the country.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Hrútsfjallstindar is a series of Icelandic peaks rising from Vatnajökull between Svínafellsjökull and Skaftafellsjökull, in its southern part.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>There are four peaks, which range from 1,756 metres (5,761 ft) to 1,875 metres (6,152 ft) high.[6]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The average thickness of the ice is 380 m (1,250 ft),[1] with a maximum thickness of 950 m (3,120 ft).[5] Iceland's highest peak, Hvannadalshnjúkur (2,109.6 m or 6,921 ft 3 in), as part of the Öræfajökull, is in the southern periphery of Vatnajökull, near Skaftafell.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Under the ice cap, as under many of the glaciers of Iceland, there are several volcanoes.[2] Eruptions from these volcanoes have led to the development of large pockets of water beneath the ice, which may burst the weakened ice and cause a jökulhlaup (glacial lake outburst flood).[2] During the last ice age, numerous volcanic eruptions occurred under Vatnajökull, creating many subglacial eruptions.[7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>An Icelandic older name for Vatnajökull was Klofajökull [ˈkʰlɔːvaˌjœːkʏtl̥] (Cleft Glacier, due to cuts into the ice several of which can be presumed to be liable for the name), which is known from eighteenth-century sources such as the writings of Eggert Ólafsson and Bjarni Pálsson.[10] In September 1950, a Douglas DC-4 operated by the private airline Loftleiðir crash-landed on the Vatnajökull glacier.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The entire six-person crew survived. A rescue operation was launched after the crew managed to send a distress signal on the fourth day. The crew and the rescue team walked the 34 km to safety.[11]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2004, Vatnajökull was one of several Icelandic settings visited on the first leg of The Amazing Race 6.[13]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Vatnajökull has around 30 outlet glaciers flowing from the ice cap.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Icelandic term for glacier is "jökull", and so is the term for outlet glacier.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Given below is a list of outlet glaciers flowing from Vatnajökull, sorted by the four administrative territories of Vatnajökull National Park.[17][18] This is not a complete list.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2025, the average air temperature surrounding Vatnajökull reached a low of -1.09 degrees Celsius in January and a high of 0.97 degrees Celsius in December.[19] In comparison to fifty years prior, in 1975, the average air temperature reached a low of -1.50 degrees Celsius in July and a high of 0.45 degrees Celsius in December.[20] While there has been an increase in the average lowest air temperatures and average highest air temperatures, the impacts of atmospheric warming have been mitigated by the Cold Blob, sometimes referred to as the Blue Blog, which is a patch of cold water in the North Atlantic Ocean slowing glacier melting in Iceland.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Vatnajökull is the second largest ice cap in Europe by volume, being about 3,000 km3 (720 cu mi)[1] and area (after the still larger Severny Island ice cap of Novaya Zemlya, Russia, which is in the extreme northeast of Europe).[1] On 7 June 2008, it became a part of the Vatnajökull National Park.[4]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

In more modern times, the volcanoes continue to erupt beneath the glaciers, resulting in many documented floods. <<Q_RELEVANT>>One jökulhlaup in 1934 caused the release of 15 km3 (3+1⁄2 cu mi) of water over the course of several days.[7] The volcanic lake Grímsvötn was the source of a large jökulhlaup in 1996.[8] There was also a considerable but short-lived eruption of the volcano under these lakes at the beginning of November 2004.[9] On 21 May 2011 a volcanic eruption started in Grímsvötn in Vatnajökull National Park at around 19:00.[9] The plume reached up to 17 km (56,000 ft).[9]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The glacier was used as the setting for the opening sequence (set in Siberia) of the 1985 James Bond film A View to a Kill, in which Bond (played for the last time by Roger Moore) eliminated a host of armed villains before escaping in a submarine to Alaska.[12] Several other films, including another in the Bond franchise, have been filmed on or using Jökulsárlón, the terminal lake of the Breiðamerkurjökull outlet from Vatnajökull.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Westlife's official music video for their twenty-fifth single top 10 and #2 UK hit in 2009 "What About Now" is the last film of Vatnajökull Glacier before the subsequent volcanic eruption.[14]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2013, Vatnajökull was a scenic background in the movie Interstellar[16], directed and produced by Christopher Nolan.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

When the island was first settled, it was extensively forested, with around 30% of the land covered in trees. In the late 12th century, Ari the Wise described it in the Íslendingabók as "forested from mountain to sea shore".[97] Permanent human settlement greatly disturbed the isolated ecosystem of thin, volcanic soils and limited species diversity. The forests were heavily exploited over the centuries for firewood and timber.[98] Deforestation, climatic deterioration during the Little Ice Age, and overgrazing by sheep imported by settlers caused a loss of critical topsoil due to erosion. Today, many farms have been abandoned. <<QA_RELEVANT>>Three-quarters of Iceland's 100,000 square kilometres (39,000 mi2) is affected by soil erosion; 18,000 km2 (6,900 sq mi) is affected to a degree serious enough to make the land useless.[97] Only a few small birch stands now exist in isolated reserves.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Icelandic Forest Service and other forestry groups promote large-scale reforestation in the country.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Due to the reforestation efforts, the forest cover of Iceland has increased sixfold since the 1990s.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>That helps to offset carbon emissions, prevent sandstorms, and increase the productivity of farms.[99] The planting of new forests has increased the number of trees, but the result does not compare to the original forests.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Some of the planted forests include introduced species.[98] The tallest tree in Iceland is a sitka spruce planted in 1949 in Kirkjubæjarklaustur; it was measured at 25.2 m (83 ft) in 2013.[100] Algae including Chondrus crispus, Phyllphora truncata, Phyllophora crispa, and others have been recorded from Iceland.[101]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Many fjords punctuate Iceland's 4,970-kilometre-long (3,090 mi) coastline, which is also where most settlements are situated.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The island's interior, the Highlands of Iceland, is a cold and uninhabitable combination of sand, mountains, and lava fields.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The major towns are the capital city of Reykjavík, along with its outlying towns of Kópavogur, Hafnarfjörður, and Garðabær, nearby Reykjanesbær where the international airport is located, and the town of Akureyri in northern Iceland.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The island of Grímsey on the Arctic Circle contains the northernmost habitation of Iceland, whereas Kolbeinsey contains the northernmost point of Iceland.[77] Iceland has three national parks: Vatnajökull National Park, Snæfellsjökull National Park, and Þingvellir National Park.[78] The country is considered a "strong performer" in environmental protection.[79]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Iceland[d] is a Nordic island country between the Arctic Ocean and the North Atlantic Ocean, located on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge between Europe and North America.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is culturally and politically linked with Europe and is the region's westernmost and most sparsely populated country.[10] Its capital and largest city is Reykjavík, which is home to about 35% of the country's roughly 395,000 residents (excluding nearby towns/suburbs, which are separate municipalities).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The official language of the country is Icelandic.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Iceland is on a rift between tectonic plates, and its geologic activity includes geysers and frequent volcanic eruptions.[11][12] The interior consists of a volcanic plateau with sand and lava fields, mountains and glaciers, and many glacial rivers flow to the sea through the lowlands.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Iceland is warmed by the Gulf Stream and has a temperate climate, despite being at a latitude just south of the Arctic Circle.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Its latitude and marine influence keep summers chilly, and most of its islands have a polar climate.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>According to the Landnámabók, an ancient manuscript, the settlement of Iceland began in 874 AD, when the Norwegian chieftain Ingólfr Arnarson became the island's first permanent settler.[13] In following centuries, Norwegians and to a lesser extent other Scandinavians, immigrated to Iceland, bringing with them thralls (i.e., slaves or serfs) of Gaelic origin.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The island was governed as an independent commonwealth under the native parliament, the Althing, one of the world's oldest functioning legislative assemblies. <<Q_RELEVANT>>After a period of civil strife, Iceland acceded to Norwegian rule in the 13th century.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1397, Iceland followed Norway's integration into the Kalmar Union along with the kingdoms of Denmark and Sweden, coming under de facto Danish rule upon its dissolution in 1523.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Danish kingdom introduced Lutheranism by force in 1550,[14] and the Treaty of Kiel formally ceded Iceland to Denmark in 1814.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The island's present name originated from Flóki Vilgerðarson, the first Norseman to intentionally travel to Iceland.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>According to the Sagas of Icelanders, Flóki coined the name after he climbed a mountain, despondent after a harsh winter in present-day Vatnsfjörður, and saw an ice cap.[21] The notion that Iceland's settlers chose that name to discourage competing settlements is most likely a myth.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The bay, originally created by glacial activity, has two major rivers flowing into it: Skjálfandafljót, which is a glacier river, and Laxá, which is a freshwater river.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The river Laxá [ˈlaksˌauː] ("Salmon River") is famous for its salmon and part of the river is protected by the Ramsar Convention.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Skjálfandi (Icelandic pronunciation: [ˈscaulvantɪ] ⓘ; also known as Skjálfandaflói [ˈscaulvantaˌflouːɪ]) is a bay in northern Iceland, with some of the characteristics of a fjord.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Icelandic word Skjálfandi literally translates to trembling which may refer to earthquakes in the area.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The only town in Skjálfandi Bay is Húsavík, facing the snow-covered Víknafjöll [ˈvihknaˌfjœtl̥] and Kinnarfjöll [ˈcɪnːarˌfjœtl̥] mountain ranges on the other side of the bay.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The highest point reaches around 1,200 metres (3,900 ft).<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>There are two islands in Skjálfandi.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The larger one is Flatey (flat island). It is situated close to the opposite side of the bay from Húsavík. There is a village on the island, no longer inhabited, composed of a few houses, a school and a church. There is no ferry serving Flatey. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Skjálfandi's smaller island is called Lundey.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Its name means island of the puffins because of the great colony of puffins living on its cliffs during the summer. <<A_RELEVANT>>Lundey is located 8.3 kilometres (5.2 miles) north from Húsavík.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Garðar Svavarsson was one of the first Scandinavians to settle in Iceland, doing so around 860 CE.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>He built a house in Skjálfandi, but spent only the following winter months there before leaving Iceland.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>His slave Náttfari was left behind and continued to live on the farm but was chased away from it later by a Norse settler, forcing Náttfari to build a new farm on poorer land in Náttfaravík ([ˈnauhtˌfaːraˌviːk]; Old Norse: [ˈnɑːtːˌfɑrɑˌwiːk]) by Skjálfandi.<</Q_RELEVANT>>
